## Distributed Processing  
You can run the IC Validator tool in a variety of different distributed processing situations, including using multiple CPUs on a single host and using multiple hosts.  
Running the IC Validator tool with distributed processing provides the following features:  
- Scalability increases with the number of CPUs used
- Flexibility for adding CPUs to an existing IC Validator job
- Simultaneous multithreading  
Distributed processing is described in the following sections:  
- Specifying Host Names and CPU Counts
- License Requirements

metadata.Header 2: Specifying Host Names and CPU Counts

content:
## Specifying Host Names and CPU Counts  
The IC Validator tool takes advantage of multiple CPUs on a host by determining automatically whether to start parallel tasks or multithread. You must communicate to the tool how many CPUs on the host you want to use. You can do this by using the -host\_init command-line option.  
For example, to use 8 CPUs on a single host, use the following command-line option:  
```
icv -host_init 8 runset.rs
```  
It is possible to specify which host to run on. In the preceding example, the host name was omitted, so the local host was assumed. If you specify a different host name, the ICValidator tool starts on that host. In the following example, 8 CPUs are used on hostA.  
```
icv -host_init hostA:8 runset.rs
```  
Because a remote host is specified, the IC Validator tool must make a connection to that host. By default, the tool attempts to use the rsh command to make this connection. If a different connection method is needed, use the -host\_login command-line option (some IT environments might disable rsh access or require a different connection method). In the following example, 8 CPUs are used on hostA and ssh is used to connect to the host.  
<!-- image -->  
```
icv -host_init hostA:8 -host_login /bin/ssh runset.rs
```

## Note:  
IC Validator uses rsh as the host login program by default when available. Using rsh can be considered a security risk and is frequently discouraged and disabled. If rsh is disabled in your environment, IC Validator automatically uses ssh . Disabling rsh at the system level is the recommended way to enforce the security policy for all users on your network. You can also set the -host\_login command-line option to always use ssh when launching IC Validator (for example, -host\_login ssh ).  
You can list more than one host. In this case, the IC Validator tool uses all of the hosts listed, with the number of CPUs specified. In the following example a total of 32 CPUs are used: 8 CPUs on the local host; 8 on hostA; and 16 CPUs on hostB (because the -host\_login command-line option is NOT specified, rsh connects to the hosts).  
```
icv -host_init 8 hostA:8 hostB:16 runset.rs
```  
You can enable additional threads on the hosts that support simultaneous multithreading (SMT). In the following example, on a host with two logical CPUs per core, the IC Validator tool dedicates 8 CPUs for commands and 8 additional CPUs for threading.  
```
icv -host_init 8 -host_thread_mode SMT
```  
See the -host\_init and -host\_login command-line options in IC Validator CommandLine Options for more information.  
## Note:  
If the host name is specified but the CPU count is omitted, ALL of the CPUs are used on the host.  
After the job is running, you can add more CPUs. Hosts and CPUs are specified in the same way using the -host\_add command-line option. Notice that this job must be run from the same working directory as the original IC Validator job. If the run\_details directory was specified in the initial run using -rd , this directory must also be specified on this run using -rd .

metadata.Header 2: Modifying Resources for a Running Job

content:
## Modifying Resources for a Running Job  
You can add more CPUs to a running IC Validator job. Hosts and CPUs are specified with the -host\_add command-line option, in the same way that they are specified with the -host\_init command-line option.  
The following example adds 16 CPUs on hostC to the running job.  
```
icv -host_add hostC:16
```

## Note:  
When using -host\_add , most of the other command-line options are unnecessary and not allowed. See -host\_add in Table3 for more information.  
You can also remove hosts from a running job. Hosts are specified using the -host\_remove command-line option. It is only possible to remove entire hosts. The following example removes all of hostC (all of its CPUs) from the running job.  
```
icv -host_remove hostC
```  
You can instruct IC Validator to automatically add and remove hosts from the running job. Hosts are added when too many commands are queued and are removed when the hosts are idle. This can be specified when the job is originally started or after the job is running. You must provide the command that IC Validator should use to acquire a new host. The command must include an icv -host\_add on the acquired host.  
For the -host\_init , -host\_add , and -host\_elastic command-line options, this IC Validator call must be run in the same working directory as the running job. Furthermore, if the run\_details directory was specified in the initial running run using -rd , this directory must also be specified on this run using -rd . All command-line options are ignored with the following exceptions: -rd is used by all three of these options, and -host\_login / -host\_disk is used by -host\_add .

## Running in LSF  
When running in LSF, the syntax and preceding examples are still appropriate. The following example shows how to launch an LSF job that starts IC Validator on 16 CPUs on a single host, using the bsub command.  
```
bsub -n 16 -R "span[ptile=16]" <bsub options> icv -host_init 16 runset.rs
```  
Similarly, to add 16 CPUs on one host to a running IC Validator job, use the -host\_add command-line option. For example,  
```
bsub -n 16 -R "span[ptile=16]" <bsub options> icv -host_add 16
```  
As a convenience, the IC Validator tool can automatically determine the host configuration and sets -host\_login to blaunch . To enable this feature, specify LSF as the as the argument to -host\_init . In the following example, 16 CPUs are requested on a single host using bsub and are identified using the LSF argument of the -host\_init commandline option.  
```
bsub -n 16 -R "span[ptile=16]" <bsub options> icv -host_init LSF runset.rs
```  
<!-- image -->  
<!-- image -->  
This feature is most useful when requesting jobs on multiple hosts. The following example works with multiple hosts as well (2 hosts, 16 CPUs each):  
```
bsub -n 32 -R "span[ptile=16]" <bsub options> icv -host_init LSF runset.rs
```  
The LSF argument also works with the -host\_add command-line option. In this example, a total of 64 CPUs are added to a running job: 8 hosts each with 8 CPUs.  
```
bsub -n 64 -R "span[ptile=8]" <bsub options> icv -host_add LSF
```  
To elastically add hosts to the job, specify a bsub command to the host\_elastic command-line option that acquires a machine and starts the IC Validator tool. In the following example, a single host is requested with 8 CPUs. (Depending on your environment, you might need to provide additional arguments to bsub.)  
```
bsub -n 8 'span[hosts=1]' icv -host_add LSF
```  
Add this entire string to the host\_elastic command-line option or specify in a separate script. The complete IC Validator command can look as follows:  
```
icv -host_init 16 -host_elastic "bsub -n 8 'span[hosts=1]' icv -host_add LSF" runset.rs
```

## Running in Univa Grid Engine (UGE/SGE)  
When running in SGE, the syntax and preceding examples are still appropriate. The following example shows how to launch an SGE job that starts IC Validator on 16 CPUs on a single host using the qsub command.  
```
qsub -pe mt 16 <qsub options> icv -host_init 16 runset.rs
```  
Similarly, to add 16 CPUs on one host to a running IC Validator job, use the -host\_add command-line option. For example,  
```
qsub -pe mt 16  <qsub options> icv -host_add 16
```  
As a convenience, the IC Validator tool can automatically determine the host configuration and sets -host\_login to qrsh -inherit . To enable this feature, specify SGE as the argument to -host\_init . In the following example, 16 CPUs are requested on a single host using qsub and are identified using the SGE argument of the -host\_init commandline option.  
```
qsub -mt 16 < qsub options> icv -host_init SGE runset.rs
```  
This feature is most useful when requesting jobs on multiple hosts. The following example works with multiple hosts as well (2 hosts, 16 CPUs each):  
```
qsub -pe dp16 32 <qsub options> icv -host_init SGE runset.rs
```  
<!-- image -->  
The SGE argument also works with the -host\_add command-line option. In this example, a total of 64 CPUs are added to a running job: 8 hosts each with 8 CPUs.  
```
qsub -pe dp8 64 <qsub options> icv -host_add SGE
```  
To elastically add hosts to a running job, use the host\_elastic command-line option with a qsub command that requests a machine and launches IC Validator. For example, to request a single host with 8 CPUs, use the following command:  
```
qsub -cwd -V -pe mt 8 icv -host_add SGE
```  
Include this entire string as the argument to the host\_elastic option, or specify it in a separate script. The complete IC Validator command can look like the following:  
```
icv -host_init 16 -host_elastic "qsub -cwd -V -pe mt 8 icv -host_add SGE" runset.rs
```

## Running in SLURM  
When running in SLURM, the syntax and preceding examples are still appropriate. The following example shows how to launch an SLURM job that starts IC Validator on 16 CPUs on a single host using the sbatch command.  
```
sbatch --cpus-per-task=16 --nodes=1 <sbatch options> run_add.sh run_icv.sh: icv -host_init 16 runset.rs (or) icv -host_init SLURM runset.rs
```  
Similarly, to add 16 CPUs on one host to a running IC Validator job, use the -host\_add command-line option. For example,  
```
sbatch --cpus-per-task=16 --nodes 1 <sbatch options> run_add.sh run_add.sh: icv -host_add 16 (or) icv -host_add SLURM
```  
As a convenience, the IC Validator tool can automatically determine the host configuration and set -host\_login to srun with the appropriate command-line options. To enable this feature, specify SLURM as the argument to -host\_init . For example, to request 16 CPUs on a single host using sbatch :  
```
sbatch --cpus-per-task=16 --nodes 1 <sbatch options> run_icv.sh run_icv.sh: icv -host_init SLURM runset.rs
```  
<!-- image -->  
This feature is most useful when requesting jobs on multiple hosts. The following example works with multiple hosts as well (2 hosts, 16 CPUs each):  
```
sbatch --cpus-per-task=16 --nodes 2 <sbatch options> run_icv.sh run_icv.sh: icv -host_init SLURM runset.rs
```  
Similarly, for adding hosts to a running job, use:  
```
icv -host_add SLURM
```  
To elastically add hosts to a running job, use the host\_elastic command-line option with an sbatch command that requests a machine and launches IC Validator. For example, to request a single host with 8 CPUs, use the following command:  
```
sbatch --cpus-per-task=8 --nodes 1 <sbatch options> run_add.sh run_add.sh: icv -host_add SLURM
```  
Include this entire string as the argument to the host\_elastic option, or specify it in a separate script. The complete IC Validator command can look like the following:  
```
icv -host_init 16 -host_elastic "sbatch --cpus-per-task=8 --nodes 1 <sbatch options> run_add.sh" runset.rs
```

## Runset Caching  
The IC Validator runset caching feature reduces the startup time of the ICValidator tool. After a runset is parsed and optimized, the internal data structures for the runset are saved to a runset cache file. Subsequent ICValidator runs that use the same runset load the runset cache file rather than parsing and optimizing the runset again.  
You can turn runset caching off by using the -norscache command-line option. You might want to use this option when debugging a run.

## Note:  
If you use runset caching with parasitic extraction (PEX) functions for multiple corners, the ICValidator tool does not flag any file naming conflicts until runtime.  
See Using IC Validator Command-Line Options With Runset Caching on page72 for information about using command-line options with runset caching.

## Cache Files  
When the ICValidator tool writes a runset cache file, the following messages are written to screen indicating the path of the cache file:  
```
Saved runset to cache: /remote/us54h1/myname/.icvrscache/ e3b32d5de337d888106672bbba370041-rod-3908.rscache Parsing Finished Runset Compile Time=0:00:03 User=3.37 Sys=0.16 Mem=0.182 GB
```  
When the ICValidator tool reads a runset cache file, the following messages are written to the screen indicating the path of the cache file that was read:  
```
Loaded runset from cache: /remote/us54h1/myname/.icvrscache/ e3b32d5de337d888106672bbba370041-rod-3908.rscache Cached Runset Compile Time=0:00:00 User=0.25 Sys=0.04 Mem=0.108 GB
```  
You can determine which cache file in your cache directory is associated with a specific runset. When you look at the content of the cache file, you'll see something like this text:  
```
Cached runset file created from ICV runset: /remote/seg-scratch/myname/S475264/pxl.ev
```  
. . .  
The second line is the full path of the runset that was used to generate the cache file.  
<!-- image -->

## Configuring Runset Caching  
You can use several environment variables to configure runset caching.  
```
ICV_RUNSET_CACHE_DIR_SHARED
```  
Sets the shared runset cache directory used by the IC Validator tool.  
```
% setenv ICV_RUNSET_CACHE_DIR_SHARED directory
```  
This cache directory is not user-specific. Multiple users can point to the same shared cache directory. When enabled, the ICValidator tool performs the following checks:  
- Checks the shared cache directory for cache that either matches or misses the runset criteria
- If missed, the IC Validator tool checks the local cache directory
- If matched, the IC Validator tool uses the local cache file.
- If missed, the IC Validator tool compiles and stores cache in the local cache directory (local to the user).  
You must move cache files to the shared directory manually so that they can be used by multiple users.  
```
ICV_RUNSET_CACHE_DIR
```  
Sets the runset cache directory used by the ICValidator tool when storing cache files.  
```
% setenv ICV_RUNSET_CACHE_DIR directory
```  
The default runset cache directory is ~/.icvrscache.  
Runset cache directories are user-specific. That is, multiple users cannot point to the same runset cache directory by setting their ICV\_RUNSET\_CACHE\_DIR variables to the same directory.  
```
ICV_RUNSET_CACHE_MAXFILES
```  
Limits the number of runset cache files that the ICValidator tool writes to the runset cache directory.  
```
% setenv ICV_RUNSET_CACHE_MAXFILES num_files_to_keep
```  
When the ICValidator tool is run, it does not delete any preexisting runset cache files until either the ICV\_RUNSET\_CACHE\_MAXFILES or the ICV\_RUNSET\_CACHE\_MAXSIZE limit is reached. When either limit is reached, the ICValidator tool deletes files in the least-recently used order; that is, cache files that have been loaded recently are retained while the older files are deleted.  
<!-- image -->  
<!-- image -->  
```
ICV_RUNSET_CACHE_MAXSIZE
```  
Limits the amount of disk space the ICValidator tool can use to store runset cache files. By default, the IC Validator tool limits the space used for runset cache files to 200 MB.  
```
% setenv ICV_RUNSET_CACHE_MAXSIZE max_size
```  
The max\_size value is a numeric value followed by an optional letter indicating the unit type. You can use a unit type of K for kilobytes, M for megabytes, G for gigabytes, or T for terabytes. If no unit type is used, the max\_size value is assumed to be in megabytes.  
```
ICV_RUNSET_CACHE_DEBUG
```  
Reports messages that help you pinpoint a configuration problem or the source of the unexpected behavior. Use this variable if runset caching is behaving in an unexpected way. The messages show configuration parameters and give a reason for loading or not loading each candidate cache file in the runset cache directory.

You can also use the -norscache command-line option.

metadata.Header 2: Matching a Runset to a Cache File

content:
## Matching a Runset to a Cache File  
The ICValidator tool matches a runset to an existing runset cache file only when the following criteria are met:  
- Preprocessing directives must match the directives stored in the cache file. Some of these directives are internally generated by the ICValidator tool, but others come directly from the ICValidator command line via the -D , -U , and -I options.
- The -svn , -uvn , -svc , -uvc , -sfn , and -ufn command-line options have not changed between runs.
- The preprocessed runset must match that of the cache file, as determined by a hashing algorithm.
- The current ICValidator version must match that of the cache file.
- The endianness of the architectures that IC Validator is run on during the cache save and the current run (the cache load attempt) must match. For example, AIX and Sun are big endian platforms and, therefore, can share a cache file.
- UNIX environment variables referenced in the runset must have the same values as they had when the cache file was generated.

## Note:  
Using the -ln and -lnf to override file names and formats specified in the layout\_file argument of the read\_layout\_net() function does not cause cache misses.

metadata.Header 2: Running Knowledge Assistant Using IC Validator

content:
## Running Knowledge Assistant Using IC Validator  
To launch the IC Validator Knowledge Assistant from the command line, use the icv -copilot command.  
Before running this command, ensure that the SNPSAI\_COPILOT\_HOME environment variable is correctly set. If the snpsai\_copilot binary cannot be located through the SNPSAI\_COPILOT\_HOME environment variable or the system's search path, IC Validator displays the following error message and terminates:  
Error: 'snpsai\_copilot' could not be found in env var SNPSAI\_COPILOT\_HOME  
No additional command-line arguments should be used with the -copilot option, as any extra arguments are ignored.  
You can run the Knowledge Assistant in the foreground using icv -copilot or in the background using icv -copilot & . After approximately 10-15 seconds, the Knowledge Assistant is launched, as shown in Figure3.  
<!-- image -->  
Figure 3 IC Validator Knowledge Assistant  
<!-- image -->  
IC Validator automatically exits when you close the Knowledge Assistant GUI.  
The IC Validator Knowledge Assistant verifies the presence of any valid IC Validator license but does not check out an IC Validator license. Instead, it checks out a GenAI\_KA\_Copilot license to operate.

metadata.Header 2: Using IC Validator Command-Line Options With Runset Caching

content:
## Using IC Validator Command-Line Options With Runset Caching  
After a runset is run the first time with runset caching enabled, subsequent runs of the same runset normally result in a cache file being read rather than a full parse of the runset.  
The content of the runset can be altered by certain ICValidator command-line options, which affects the use of runset caching. These changes cause the ICValidator tool to write a new cache. Anytime the runset is modified, runset caching are affected.

## Note:  
Options not specifically mentioned in the following sections are generally compatible with runset caching.  
<!-- image -->

## Compatible Command-Line Options  
The following ICValidator options are compatible with runset caching. These options can be added, removed, or modified on the command line. The ICValidator tool still uses the previously generated cache.  
- -c
- -g
- -i
- -p
- -f
- -rd
- -stc

metadata.Header 2: Command-Line Options That Affect Runset Caching

content:
## Command-Line Options That Affect Runset Caching  
The following options cause changes in the content of the preprocessed runset. Therefore, when you add these options to the command line or change their arguments, the preprocessed runset does not hash to the same cache file. The runset parses normally and writes a new cache file. If these options are not changed, subsequent runs of the same runset hash to this cache file.  
- -64
- -D
- -U
- -il
- -iln
- -sfn
- -svc
- -svn
- -ufn
- -uvc
- -uvn
- -verbose  
<!-- image -->

## Incompatible Command-Line Options  
Because of the unique flows used to handle the following options, these options disable runset caching when used:  
```
-debug -debug_source -ndg
```  
The following option affects runset caching because it changes internal options in the parser. When you use this option, the ICValidator tool generates a separate cache file:  
-nro

## Layer Mapping  
There are two types of layer mapping:  
- Runset Layer Mapping: This mapping modifies your runset to create a new runset.
- Data Layer Mapping: This mapping modifies the data as it is read in by changing the layer and datatype attributes of the data.  
You can use both types of mapping when you are running on multiple libraries.

## Runset Layer Mapping  
Runset layer mapping is the process of substituting layer/datatype numbers that are specified in the ASSIGN section of a runset with the actual layer/datatype numbers of data in a database. You need to map layers, for example, when the layer/datatype numbers in your database are not consistent with the layer/datatype numbers specified in a foundry supplied runset.  
Specify the mapping file with the -lf command-line option -if com and l e pt . See IC Validator CommandLine Options on page25.  
The first line of the mapping file must always be  
```
RUNSET(*,*) = Library(*,*)
```  
This statement maps each layer to itself (identity mapping). This identity mapping ensures that there is a mapping for each layer. Subsequent lines of the mapping file override the identity map for selected layers.  
<!-- image -->

## For example,  
```
Runset(*,*) = Library(*,*) Runset(15,0) = Library(1,0) Runset(16,0) = Library(2,0) Runset(17,0) = Library(3,0)
```  
Mapping is specified within the file using the following formats:

## Note:  
Runset(i,j) refers to layer/datatype numbers in the ASSIGN section of the runset.  
Library(i,j) refers to the actual layer/datatype numbers of the data in the database.  
```
· Runset(A,B) = Library(C,D)
```  
In the following example, an assign reference to layer/datatype (1,5) is replaced with layer/datatype (2,0).  
```
Runset(1,5) = Library(2,0) · Runset(A,B) = Library(C1...Cm,D1...Dn)
```  
In the following example, any assign reference to layer/datatype (5,0) is replaced with the four layer/datatype pairs (10,0), (10,4), (12,0), and (12,4).  
```
Runset(5,0) = Library(10 12,0 4) · Runset(A1...Am,B1...Bn) = Library(C1...Cm,D1...Dn)
```  
## Note:  
The number of Runset layer elements and Library layer elements must be equal.  
The number of Runset datatype elements and Library datatype elements must be equal.  
In the following example, four layer/datatype substitutions are made:  
```
assign (2,6) is replaced with (10,0) assign (2,8) is replaced with (10,4) assign (4,6) is replaced with (12,0) assign (4,8) is replaced with (12,4) Runset(2 4,6 8) = Library(10 12,0 4)
```  
<!-- image -->  
The syntax rules for a mapping file are  
- Wildcards are allowed in place of a list. For example,  
```
Runset(1,*) = Library(2,*)
```  
means that assign layer 1, all datatypes, is replaced with layer 2, all datatypes.  
- Layer/datatype ranges are specified by a dash. For example,
- List elements must be in ascending order.  
```
Runset(2 5-8,*) = Library(10-12 17 20,*)
```  
When the ICValidator tool is executed with a layer mapping file, any substitution of assign layer/datatype numbers is reported below the assign statement in the cell .sum file. Here is an example report:  
```
L1_all = assign({ { 11 } }) Function: assign Inputs: L1_all.polygonlayer.0001 Outputs: L1_all.polygonlayer.0002 Layer list {{11}} was replaced with {{1}}
```

## Data Layer Mapping  
Use data layer mappings when you merge multiple libraries with corresponding data on different layers or datatypes. For example, if you have a main design library with metal1 on layer 41 and a secondary library with metal1 on layer 31, you need to merge these libraries using data layer mapping so that all metal1 data is read in on the same layer. This layer is layer41 in this example.  
Typically, you specify the main design library with the library() function. The library() function does not provide data layer mapping capabilities for the main library. However, data layer mapping is available when you specify additional libraries. Therefore, you can map the data from the additional libraries to the corresponding layers and datatypes used by the main design library.  
If you use the library\_create() function instead of the library() function, all of the libraries are specified with the library\_import() function and have data layer mapping available. For the purposes of data layer mapping, you can use any library as the main library and layer map the remaining libraries to that main library.  
In addition to data layer mapping, you can also use runset layer mapping in the same run to map the runset layers to the layers used by your main library. The following examples illustrate this scenario.  
<!-- image -->  
<!-- image -->  
In this example, the main and secondary libraries are specified in the library() function:  
- The main library, one.oasis, is specified with the library() function. It has metal1 on layer 41.
- A secondary library, two.oasis, has metal1 on layer 31.
- The runset assumes that metal1 is on layer 5.  
The metal1 data on layer 31 in the two.oasis library is mapped to layer 41 as it is read in. This mapping ensures that all input metal1 data is read onto layer 41. The runset layer mapping then transforms the assign({{5}}) assignment into assign({{41}}) to ensure that the run executes as expected. Here is a snippet of the runset:  
```
library(library_name = "one.oasis", cell= "A", format= OASIS, merge_libraries = {{library_name = "two.oasis", format=OASIS, layer_map_file="two_layer_map"}}); metal1= assign({{5}});
```  
The two\_layer\_map file has the data layer mapping for two.oasis:  
```
4131
```  
The runset layer mapping file, specified with the -lf command-line option, has this mapping:  
```
RUNSET(*,*) = LIBRARY(*,*) RUNSET(5,*) = LIBRARY(41,*)
```  
In the following example, the main library is specified in the library() function and the secondary library in the library\_import() function. Use this method to import multiple libraries when you do not want cell merging to occur. Each library remains distinct from the others so that your assigns functions can import data from one library but not another.  
- The main library, one.oasis, is specified with the library() function. It has metal1 on layer 41.
- A secondary library, two.gds, has metal1 on layer 31.
- The runset assumes that metal1 is on layer 5.  
The two\_layer\_map file and the runset layer mapping are the same as in the previous example. Here is a snippet of the runset:  
```
lib1 = library(library_name = "one.oasis", cell= "A", format= OASIS); lib2 = library_import(library_name= "two.gds",
```  
```
cell= "A", cell_prefix= "TWO_", format= GDSII, layer_map_file = "two_layer_map"); metal1 = assign({{5}});
```  
In the following example, the main library is specified in the library() function and the secondary library in the milkyway\_merge\_library\_options() function. The libraries are not merged nor kept separate. Milkyway cell data is replaced with the equivalent GDSII data on a cell-by-cell basis. See the milkyway\_merge\_library\_options() function for more information.  
- The main Milkyway library, one, is specified with the library() function. It has metal1 on layer 41.
- A secondary GDSII library, two.gds, has metal1 on layer 31.
- The runset assumes that metal1 is on layer 5.  
The two\_layer\_map file and the runset layer mapping are the same as in the first example. Here is a snippet of the runset:  
```
library(library_name = "one", cell= "A", format= MILKYWAY, library_path = "./"); milkyway_merge_library_options( libraries = {{"one", "./", {{"two.gds", GDSII, layer_map_file="two_layer_map"}}}}, missing_cell = ABORT); metal1 = assign({{5}});
```

## Using PXL Runset Encryption  
Runset encryption is a method used to conceal the content of the runset from an end user. Use encryption to limit the end user's knowledge of foundry process parameters or of the steps necessary to perform certain design rule checks or transformations.

## Operation  
After a runset is created as plain text, certain content can be transformed into encrypted blocks. The content of the encryption blocks can contain PXL constructs and any of the standard preprocessor directives. Plain text is also referred to as clear text.  
The pxlcry t u i pxlcrypt utility is used to encrypt the runsets. It encrypts only blocks of cleartext. This utility is included in the IC Validator release install directory. The syntax is  
<!-- image -->  
```
% pxlcrypt cleartext_runset encrypted_runset
```  
The pxlcrypt utility cannot reverse the encryption process.  
The encrypted runset is then delivered to the end user, who executes the ICValidator tool using it.  
All runset functions that are encrypted are reported as 'encrypted function' in the summary file and on standard output when the -verbose option is used. Although the functions are listed as encrypted functions, the machine usage, number of polygons generated, and names of smart-deleted layers (layers that are no longer needed because nothing depends on them) are still reported.

## Encryption Directives  
#pragm PXL enc y t [ ] io d v s The directives that mark the beginning and ending points of an encryption section are  
```
#pragma PXL encrypt begin #pragma PXL encrypt end
```  
More than one section of a runset can be encrypted in a runset. However, an encrypted section cannot be within another encrypted section. Here is an example of an encryption section in a runset:  
```
... #pragma PXL encrypt begin e2 @= { @ "e2 violation"; external2( l1, l2, distance < 2.0, extension = NONE, look_thru = COINCIDENT);} #pragma PXL encrypt end ...
```  
Partial constructs cannot be encrypted. For example, this partial construct is not allowed:  
```
... external2( l1, l2, distance < 2.0, extension = NONE, #pragma PXL encrypt begin look_thru = COINCIDENT);} #pragma PXL encrypt end ...
```  
The pxlcrypt utility automatically breaks encryption blocks around included files. For example, if the runset has this code:  
```
#pragma PXL encrypt begin ... #include "file1.rh" ... #pragma PXL encrypt end
```  
<!-- image -->

metadata.Header 2: Then, the code is encrypted as:

content:
## Then, the code is encrypted as:  
```
#pragma PXL encrypt begin ... #pragma PXL encrypt end #include "file1.rh" #pragma PXL encrypt begin ... #pragma PXL encrypt end
```

## Licensing and Resource Requirements  
This chapter contains the setup instructions for the IC Validator tool. Make sure that you have all the correct directories and files, that your environment accommodates the ICValidator tool, and that you have incorporated the proper licensing information.  
The licensing and resource requirements are described in the following sections:  
- Licensing Schemes
- License Waiting
- Which IC Validator Licenses Do I Need?
- Resource Requirements  
For additional information about Synopsys licensing and installing the ICValidator tool, see the following documents:  
- The Synopsys Licensing QuickStart Guide, available at http://www.synopsys.com/Support/LI/Licensing/Pages.
- Information about instal g IC V d or installing the ICValidator tool is available at http://www.synopsys.com/Support/LI/Installation/Pages/default.aspx.

## Licensing Schemes  
The IC Validator tool has three types of licensing schemes. The IC Validator tool is run using one of these schemes:  
- Apex Licensing
- Elite Licensing
- Base Licensing  
Base licensing is the default scheme. If the job does not use license waiting or the -lic\_apex , -lic\_elite , or -lic\_base command-line options, the IC Validator tool first checks for the lowest tier license required for the run and if not available then checks higher tiers. If the run can use any tier, it first checks for Base licenses. If Base licenses are not available, the tool checks for Elite, and then Apex licenses. If none of these licenses are available, the job ends with a license denied error.  
<!-- image -->  
The three licensing schemes can exist on a system as available licensing schemes, but an ICValidator job uses only one of them. They cannot be used together.  
If multiple licenses are available, you can use the -lic\_apex , -lic\_elite or -lic\_base command-line options to select the licensing scheme to use for a specific job. See IC Validator Command-Line Options on page25 for more information.

## License Waiting  
licens wa t gICV\_L ENS WA T v ro m b The IC Validator tool supports license waiting in accordance with the standard Synopsys Common Licensing (SCL) guidelines.  
When you run the IC Validator tool with license waiting,  
- If only Apex licensing is installed, the job queues for Apex licenses.
- If only Elite licensing is installed, the job queues for Elite licenses.
- If only Base licensing is installed, the job queues for Base licenses.
- If multiple licensing schemes are installed, the job queues for the first of Base, Elite, or Apex that is installed. Other schemes are ignored.
- If you use the -lic\_base command-line option, the job queues for Base licenses and the Apex and Elite licenses are ignored.
- If you use the -lic\_elite command-line option, the job queues for Elite licenses and the Apex and Base licenses are ignored.
- If you use the -lic\_apex command-line option, the job queues for Apex licenses and the Elite and Base licenses are ignored.

## User Controls  
The IC Validator tool provides user controls for when not all multicore licenses are available at the time a job is submitted.  
License\_wait\_duration. Specifies the maximum time the tool waits for licenses to become available.  
License\_mode. Determines what happens when multicore licenses are not all available at startup.  
<!-- image -->  
- run\_available . The job runs with the partial subset of licenses that is available.
- If the -license\_wait\_duration command-line option is also set and no licenses are available, the job queues for a license until a non-zero quantity is available, and then runs with those licenses.
- run\_and\_add . The job runs with the partial subset of licenses that is available, and then queues and adds as licenses become available, attempting to achieve all requested licenses.
- If the -license\_wait\_duration command-line option is also set and no licenses are available, the job queues for licenses until a non-zero quantity is available, and then starts with those licenses. The job then queues and adds as licenses become available, attempting to achieve all requested licenses.
- exit . The job exits if the full quantity is not available.
- If the -license\_wait\_duration command-line option is also set, the job queues and incrementally acquires licenses, and starts if the full quantity of licenses is achieved before the duration expires; otherwise the job exits.
- exit\_and\_retry . The job exits if the full quantity is not available, releases any licenses acquired, and retries.
- If the -license\_wait\_duration command-line option is also set, the job queues and incrementally acquires licenses, and starts if full quantity is achieved before the duration expires; otherwise, the job exits, release any licenses acquired, and retries.

## License Caching  
The IC Validator tool caches information as it learns about which license keys are installed on which license servers. In subsequent runs, the cached information might be used to change the order of the license server list used by the job or the order in which the various license schemes are checked, potentially reducing the time it takes to successfully check out licenses for the job.  
The cached information expires periodically and is also updated as the tool learns more about which licenses are available on which servers. When the tool changes the priority of license servers or license schemes, it is logged in run\_details/licmsg.  
By default, the license cache is in the following directory:  
$XDG\_CACHE\_HOME/Synopsys/icv/license  
If $XDG\_CACHE\_HOME is not set, the license cache is in the following directory:  
~/.cache/Synopsys/icv/license Set the ICV\_LICENSE\_CACHE\_DIR environment variable to override the location of the license cache.  
<!-- image -->  
License caching can be disabled by using the -nlc command-line option.

## Which IC Validator Licenses Do I Need?  
The IC Validator functions in your runset determine the required licenses. The following sections discuss the needed licenses:  
- Apex Licensing

## Apex Licensing  
Apex licensing uses the following keys:  
- ICValidator-Manager-Apex
- ICValidator2-GeometryEngine
- ICValidator2-CompareEngine  
The ICValidator-Manager-Apex key is checked out every time the ICValidator tool is run, and it uses a tiered licensing system, high (Apex), middle (Elite), and low (Base) depending on the technology or function.

- ICValidator-Manager

## Multicore Licensing  
The IC Validator tool has Apex, Elite, and Base Multicore licensing requirements, as shown in the following sections:

## Apex Multicore Licensing  
The IC Validator tool can be run with one or more ICValidator-Manager license. Each license allows you to use up to four CPUs. For example:  
A 100 CPU job requires 25 Apex (ICValidator-Manager-Apex) licenses

## Elite Multicore Licensing  
The IC Validator tool can be run with one or more ICValidator-Manager licenses. Each license allows you to use up to four CPUs. For example:  
A 100 CPU job requires 25 Elite (ICValidator-Manager) licenses

## Base Multicore Licensing  
The IC Validator tool can be run with one or more ICValidator-Manager-2020 licenses. Each license allows you to use up to two CPUs. For example:  
A 100 CPU job requires 50 Base (ICValidator-Manager-2020) licenses  
<!-- image -->

## Token Licensing  
The token based licensing describes the approach for checking out multiple licenses. The token licensing is similar to Multicore. Multiple ICV Manager licenses are consumed based on the number of CPUs, according to a defined ratio.  
The following components contribute to the total number of licenses needed for a job.  
Total number of token licenses = (Per-CPU Flow * Multicore) + Per-Session Functionality  
- Per-CPU Flow Functionality : Depending on the type of job, a certain number of licenses are needed which multiply with the multicore licensing.
- Multicore : The number of multicore result is a defined multiplier of the Per-CPU functionality
- Per-Session Functionality : Some functionality do not multiply with multicore. They consume an additional static license quantity regardless of multicore.

## Hyperthreading  
The IC Validator tool consumes licenses until the quantity of CPUs is equal to the number of physical cores. For example:  
A 100 CPU job requires 25 Apex (ICValidator-Manager-Apex) licenses

## Hyperthreading Example  
A 20-core host with Hyperthreading enabled presents itself as 40 CPUs, where 4 CPUs = 1 license:  
8 CPUs (-host\_init 8) : Consumes 2 licenses  
12 CPUs (-host\_init 12) : Consumes 3 licenses  
16 CPUs (-host\_init 16) : Consumes 4 licenses  
20 CPUs (-host\_init 20) : Consumes 5 licenses  
24 CPUs (-host\_init 24) : Consumes 5 licenses (4 CPUs reserved for Threading)  
28 CPUs (-host\_init 28) : Consumes 5 licenses (8 CPUs reserved for Threading)  
32 CPUs (-host\_init 32) : Consumes 5 licenses (12 CPUs reserved for Threading)  
36 CPUs (-host\_init 36) : Consumes 5 licenses (16 CPUs reserved for Threading)  
40 CPUs (-host\_init 40) : Consumes 5 licenses (20 CPUs reserved for Threading)  
<!-- image -->

## Resource Requirements  
The initial database file and the files that the IC Validator tool creates and uses determine the system requirements. With some knowledge of the design to be checked, you can estimate physical memory, disk space, and possible swap ce y t m r qui n swap space requirements for your ICValidator runs.  
A contrib directory, which is included with IC Validator releases, provides scripts for analyzing IC Validator performance. The contrib directory is at the top level of the release install directory. These scripts are not supported. See the README file in the contrib directory for more information.

## Space Requirements  
The IC Validator program performs layout checking operations on group files group files that are created from the design database and stored in the group directory. The IC Validator tool first creates the primary group files, one file for each layer in an assign function of the runset. Each primary group file is a database describing that layer's existence throughout the design, maintaining all hierarchy. As the IC Validator run progresses, output files are generated from certain checks. These outputs are also written as group files. For example, the files in a group directory could be:  
| HRCHY.ERROR cont.group   | inst_indx.dat met1.group   | pgate.group poly.group   | toxcont.group via.group   |
|--------------------------|----------------------------|--------------------------|---------------------------|
| gate.group               | met2.group                 | psel.group               | well.group                |  
A general rule is to have a minimum of two to three times the space of the initial database, if it is in GDSII GDSI  file, nput da b s file format, reserved for group file creation, assuming the design has a good hierarchical style. A mostly flat design y m r qu b flat design, or one with unwanted data interactions, might require four to six times the initial database space for its group file creation. Thus, for a GDSII file database of 10MB, a minimum of 20to 30MB is required for group file creation space, if the design is hierarchical in nature. By contrast, at least 40to 60MB are required for a flat design.  
In addition to the group files, the other significant output files from the ICValidator run are the run summary files and the outp da b se fil , output database files. The summary files are the cel .LAYOUT\_ER S file cell .LAYOUT\_ERRORS and cel .sum fi cell .sum files. These files are ASCII log files that document the results of the IC Validator run on the cell named in the runset.  
The size of the cell .LAYOUT\_ERRORS file and the output database depends on the number of errors encountered in the IC Validator run. As with the group files, if the design is hierarchical, the graphic out d b se, m l w n graphical output database is smaller than the graphical output for a more flat design. The graphical output database is smaller because the ICValidator tool only needs to report perfo manc ti sh l d b u errors internal to repeated modules one time, while for a flat design the error is reported for every instance of the module.  
<!-- image -->

## Memory Usage  
You can manage the memory space needed for error output reporting by using a logical approach to locating errors. Start by running the ICValidator tool on small modules of the design and address errors as they are encountered. After the errors are fixed, run the ICValidator tool on hierarchically higher modules. Using this procedure keeps your cell .LAYOUT\_ERRORS file and output database reasonably small. Working up through the hierarchy in this way manages the use of memory needed for sy tem r qui n d c g o w h b p f x , error output storage space.  
The IC Validator tool also requires physical memory and swap ce y t m r qui n swap space to complete its checks. The tool attempts to load into memory all data required to complete the checks currently being performed. Any overflow of physical memory uses swap space. Generally speaking, any time the IC Validator program needs to access swap space, you can expect performance degradation, especially if swap space is distributed over a large network with considerable network traffic. If enough perfo manc ti s v d ugh y w physical memory is available to load all data and complete a check without accessing swap space, you can expect maximum throughput. A machine with three to four times as much memory as the GDSII file size should perform well with a hierarchical design. Flat designs require more hardware. Set the swap space so that any overflow of physical memory does not exhaust the swap space and cause the ICValidator run to terminate.  
The output cell .sum file includes a list of the memory used and the number of page f ults page faults required to complete each check. If you see that certain checks require more memory than the machine has allocated, causing large amounts of data to be swapped out to disk, you might need a machine with more memory for future runs. Example1 shows an example of the reported memory usage. The following section, Runtime and Memory Use Report, gives information about the reported runtimes and memory usage.

## Operating Systems  
The IC Validator tool supports many hardware architectures and operating systems. See the instal o gu de, k installation guide for a list of the supported operating systems:  
[http://www.synopsys.com/support/licensing-installation-computeplatforms/computeplatforms/release-specific-support.html](http://www.synopsys.com/support/licensing-installation-computeplatforms/compute-platforms/release-specific-support.html)

## System Limits  
If system limits are set incorrectly, you might encounter an error during the ICValidator run. For example, the following commands set the proper system limits for an ICValidator run on a Linux operating system. (The numerical values are in kilobytes.)  
```
unlimit filesize unlimit datasize limit descriptors 1024 limit stacksize 8192
```

## Note:  
The descriptors setting controls how many files you can have open at any time during a run.  
To verify the limits on a host, run the limit shell command.

## Networked Environments  
Accessing files over a networked environment, such as when a remote group directory is used, can degrade performance. You might observe large differences in the wall time (overall time) and total CPU time (user time plus system time) reported by the ICValidator tool.

## Note:  
These differences could also be caused by:  
- Other processes running on the same system.
- System overhead.  
NFS set ing The read- and write-transfer sizes ( rsize and wsize ) of the NFS mounts should be at least 32768. For example, for static mounts set:  
```
% mount -t nfs -o rsize=32768,wsize=32768 server:/path /mnt/nfs
```

Using cloud resources allows you to handle peak workloads, access powerful hardware, and scale your compute resources as needed. IC Validator supports multiple cloud service providers and integrates with hybrid environments, making it easier to manage large and complex designs.

## Using IC Validator in the Cloud  
The advantages of using IC Validator in the cloud is as follows:  
- Elasticity: Access virtually unlimited compute and storage resources.
- Hardware Optimization: Choose the best CPUs and GPUs for your project.
- Multi-Cloud Compatibility: Work with providers like Microsoft Azure, AWS, Google Cloud, Oracle Cloud, and HPE GreenLake.
- Pay-Per-Use: Use resources as needed and pay only for what you use.
- Seamless Hybrid Integration: Scale up with additional compute resources when required.

- Cost-Effective Instances: Use spot instances and save-and-restore features for long jobs.
- Continuous Performance Improvements: Benefit from ongoing memory and I/O optimizations.

## Hybrid Cloud  
Organizations seeking to establish or enhance a hybrid cloud environment can review various supported configurations:

## No Public Cloud Access  
When cloud connectivity is unavailable, the Synopsys Cloud platform can be used to deploy a hybrid cloud environment. Refer to the Synopsys Cloud section for additional information.

metadata.Header 2: Existing Cloud Access Without Data Mirroring and Existing Compute Grid

content:
## Existing Cloud Access Without Data Mirroring and Existing Compute Grid  
Establishing a hybrid cloud environment requires a data mirroring service. The Synopsys Data Service offers an electronic design automation-focused alternative to third-party data mirroring solutions. Details are available in the Synopsys Data Service section.  
A multi-cluster grid environment is necessary to fully leverage hybrid cloud capabilities. Consult the information technology department for guidance on configuring a multicluster grid. After assembling the required components, hybrid mode can be enabled for electronic design automation workloads.

metadata.Header 2: Existing Data Mirroring and Multi-Cluster Grid Environment

content:
## Existing Data Mirroring and Multi-Cluster Grid Environment  
In this configuration, a data mirroring service (such as NetApp FlexCache) is already implemented, and the compute grid environment (such as IBM Load Sharing Facility or Simple Linux Utility for Resource Management) supports multi-cluster operation. Most Synopsys tools operate efficiently in this environment. Tool-specific options are available for distributed execution.
