## Checking PYDB Data Correctness  
You can use the command-line utility, pydbChecker , to verify the correctness of foreign keys, indexes, views, and table data, ensuring database integrity. You can also output the count of error-polygons for debugging purposes. The utility also checks the logical consistency of PYDB by performing cross-table validations to ensure data consistency across tables and to confirm that there are no missing records or errors.  
To use this utility, run the following command directly from the <ICVWB\_INSTALL\_DIR>/bin directory:  
```
pydbChecker database [-quick-check | -integrity-check] [-print-polygon-count] [-help | -h]
```

## Arguments  
database  
Specifies the path to the input PYDB database.  
<!-- image -->  
-quick-check  
Performs a quick integrity check on the database. This option performs all the checks performed by the -integrity-check option except validating the UNIQUE constraint and ensuring that the contents of the index match the contents of the table.

## -integrity-check  
Performs a full integrity check on the database. This option checks for the following:  
- Table or index entries that are not in the correct order.
- Incorrectly formatted records.
- Missing pages.
- Missing or excess index entries.
- UNIQUE , CHECK and NOT NULL constraint errors.
- Freelist integrity.
- Sections of the database that are used more than once or not at all.  
-print-polygon-count  
If specified, prints the number of polygons for each error in the database.  
<!-- formula-not-decoded -->  
Displays command usage help.  
<!-- image -->

## Working With ASCII Error Files  
This chapter describes how to load and work with ASCII error files.  
After you load a layout, you can load its corresponding DRC error files in the IC Validator WorkBench application to quickly view and analyze DRC errors. DRC error data is overlaid on the active layout where you can easily view the errors on the layout and its details in the DRC Information window. You can then classify the errors either individually or as a group and also add comments for each error record. You can also save your session and continue working with the classification in a future session.  
The following topics cover how to view, classify, and save DRC error data.  
- Loading DRC Error Data
- Viewing DRC Error Data
- Classifying and Commenting DRC Errors
- Saving DRC Error Records

## Loading DRC Error Data  
To load DRC error data for a layout:  
1. Click File > Open and open a layout.
2. Click File > Import ASCII Error Database .  
The DRC Files dialog box opens.  
3. Select a DRC error file ( .db , .rdb , or .cdb files).
4. Click Open .  
Alternatively, you can use the drc file open filename on the command line.  
The DRC error data is loaded as a single side cell in the Side Cells window and is also loaded in the DRC Information window. The layers in the error file are loaded in the Layout Layers window as a group.  
<!-- image -->

## Viewing DRC Error Data  
When you load a DRC error file, the DRC Information window displays the violations grouped by the cell in the left pane and the individual violation records in the right pane.  
In the left pane, you can choose to display the violations grouped by the cell or by the violation. The left pane also displays a summary of the violations and their total count.  
The right pane has columns that displays the error records and their details such as the hierarchy, type of object, vertices, properties, rule description and, comments. It also displays the status of the errors and any comments that you have added.  
To navigate the DRC records, use the navigation buttons on the header of the DRC Information window. As you navigate the results or select any of the DRC records, the violations are highlighted and zoomed in to by default on the layout. You can change this by clicking and selecting to only annotate the violation and not zoom in. You can also zoom in to a violation by right-clicking a record in the right pane and choosing Go To .  
When you load a DRC error file, the DRC error data is also loaded as a side cell in the Side Cells window. You can adjust the brightness and tone of the DRC violations and the dimming of the background layout error file to easily view the errors on the layout. When you load multiple DRC error files, you can select which file you need to view in the DRC Information window by right-clicking the side cell and choosing Show in DRC Table .

## Classifying and Commenting DRC Errors  
After you load and view DRC errors, you can classify the errors by giving them a status while also providing comments in the DRC Information window. You can choose to give an error one of the following statuses: Error , Fixed , Ignore , Waive , Watch , or Unclassified .  
You can classify or add comments from either the left or right panes of the DRC Information view.  
To classify the DRC errors and add comments, do one of the following:  
- In the left pane, right-click a violation group and choose a status from the context menu, or click Comment .  
This will update all the violations in that cell group with the selected status and comment.  
If you selected Comment , then the Classify DRC Records dialog box opens. Here you can add a comment for the selected violation group and also select a status for it.  
<!-- image -->  
<!-- image -->  
- In the right pane, select one record or multiple records, right-click and choose Classify . The Classify DRC Records dialog box opens.  
You can apply a status or comment to the selected DRC records, and you can then see this information in the Status and Comment columns.

## Saving DRC Error Records  
After you classify and add comments to DRC records, you can save this information as a CBD file and load it on the corresponding layout in a future session with all the information intact.  
To save DRC error records:  
1. On the header of the DRC Information view, click the Save As button.  
The Save DRC information to file dialog box opens  
2. Save the information as CDB file.  
You can then load this .cdb file by clicking File > Import ASCII Error Database .

## Synopsys Diagnostic Platform  
This chapter describes how to collect data for the Synopsys Diagnostic Platform tool to debug runtime issues that are not reproducible in the Synopsys environment.  
The Synopsys Diagnostic Platform (SDP) tool is used to collects diagnostic data from the user environment to debug runtime issues that cannot be reproduced in the Synopsys environment. It also includes profiling information about command execution to help diagnose the performance of specific scenarios.

metadata.Header 2: Collecting Data for Synopsys Diagnostic Platform

content:
## Collecting Data for Synopsys Diagnostic Platform  
To enable SDP tool, load the SDP module:  
```
module load fwsdp
```  
To start collecting information, execute the sdp start command before running the commands that should be profiled and provide a directory path where the collected data will be stored:  
```
sdp start /path/to/storage
```  
To stop collecting information execute:  
sdp stop  
<!-- image -->  
<!-- image -->

## Setting Hotkeys in the Ribbon Mode  
When running the application in the ribbon mode, you can view and configure hotkeys from the Ribbon Options window. You can assign, remove, and reset shortcut keys for actions from the Ribbon Options window.  
To assign a shortcut key for an existing action or custom action:  
1. In the Customize the Ribbon page, double-click the Shortcut cell next to any action in the left or right pane.
2. In the shortcuts dialog box, press the combination of keys you want to assign and click Assign .  
If the key combination you entered is assigned to another action, you can choose to overwrite the existing assignment or change your key combination.  
<!-- image -->  
<!-- image -->  
Once assigned, the key combinations is displayed under Current shortcuts .  
3. Click Close and then click OK in the Ribbon Options window to apply the shortcut key combination.  
To remove or reset shortcut keys:  
- Double-click the Shortcut cell of the action.
- To remove a shortcut, select the key combination from the Current shortcut keys list and click Remove .
- To reset the shortcut key assignments to its default, click Reset .  
To import a shortcut key configuration:  
1. In the Customize the Ribbon page, click the Import/Export drop-down button.
2. Select a hotkey configuration under Shortcut configuration : Default, CC\_hotkeys, ICC\_hotkeys, or V\_hotkeys.  
The following is a list of default keyboard shortcuts in the application.

## Setting Hotkeys in the Menu Mode  
When running the application in the menu mode, click Tools > Options and select Hotkeys in the Options window. The actions are listed to the right of each hotkey. The menu mode Hotkeys page also includes additional hotkey options for Layout , FindTable , Net Tracing , lefdef , and FwIDE .  
To assign or change hotkeys using the Hotkeys page:  
- Click the cell to the right of the hotkey action and press the desired keyboard keys. You can enter more than one key for each action.  
To unassign a hotkey:  
1. Click the cell to the right of the action.
2. Right-click the cell and select Delete shortcuts .  
<!-- image -->

## Note:  
You cannot reassign the Esc key, the Ctrl+I key, or the Ctrl+W key to different hotkey designations.  
To save new, added, or modified hotkeys:  
- Use the default save command.  
For more information, see the IC Validator WorkBench Command Manual .  
To import a shortcut key configuration:  
1. Click Tools > Macro > User Hotkeys .
2. Select a hotkey configuration from the list: Default, CC\_hotkeys, ICC\_hotkeys, or V\_hotkeys.  
<!-- image -->

## Adding a Hotkeys Configuration File  
You can also add a hotkeys configuration file in the application from the menu mode or ribbon mode. To add a hotkeys configuration file, place your my\_hotkeys.tcl file in the ICVWB\_INSTALL\_DIR/etc/fw/contrib directory. The my\_hotkeys.tcl configuration file name is then included in the Shortcut configuration list from the ribbon mode or in the Tools > Macro > User Hotkeys list from the menu mode.  
After you select any item in the drop-down list, the appropriate script from ICVWB\_INSTALL\_DIR/etc/fw/contrib is executed. For example, if you select my\_hotkeys, the tool executes the ICVWB\_INSTALL\_DIR/etc/fw/contrib/ my\_hotkeys.tcl script. If that script is not found, the application tries to run the ICVWB\_INSTALL\_DIR/etc/fw/contrib/my\_hotkeys.mac .

## OASIS Files Compliance Checking  
This appendix describes the standalone oasis\_info utility used to check the compliance of OASIS files or to print records in the OASIS files from the terminal window.  
This topic is available:  
- The oasis\_info Utility

## The oasis\_info Utility  
This utility returns statistics if the input OASIS file is compliant with the OASIS specification. The utility can also print partial or all records in the given OASIS file based on the arguments you specify. The utility is available in the ICVWB\_INSTALL\_DIR/bin directory and must be run from the terminal window.

## Syntax  
```
oasis_info oasis_file [-checksum | -file_props | -cblock_offset_dump] oasis_info oasis_file -all [-short [ num_points ]] [-beautify] oasis_info oasis_file [-cblock offset ] [-offset begin [ end ]] [-short [ num_points ]] [-beautify] oasis_info oasis_file -brief oasis_info oasis_file -cell cell_name [-short [ num_points ]] [-beautify]
```

## Returns  
If you do not specify any arguments, then the utility reports whether the OASIS file complies with the OASIS specification. If you specify arguments, then the utility returns additional information about the OASIS file.

## Arguments  
```
oasis_file Specifies the input OASIS file.
```  
<!-- image -->  
```
-all
```  
Specifies to return all records in the file.  
```
-beautify
```  
Specifies to break the record into multiple lines if the point list is too long. If you do not specify this option, then the utility prints the record on one line.

## -brief  
Specifies to return only the START and END records. This option does not validate the file.  
```
-cblock_offset_dump
```  
Specifies to print all CBLOCK records and offsets. Cannot combine with other options.  
```
-cblock offset
```  
Specifies to return the records in the CBLOCK record at file offset offset . If -offset offset is used with the -cblock argument, then only the records in the specified range within the CBLOCK are reported.  
```
-cell cell_name
```  
Specifies to return all records specified in the cell cell\_name .  
```
-checksum
```  
Specifies to run only a checksum calculation on OASIS files that have CRC32 or CHECKSUM32, and returns a pass or fail report. When specifying this option, the utility does NOT compute any other OASIS compliance checks.  
```
-file_props
```  
Returns file-level property records. With this option, oasis\_info does not perform deep validation.  
```
-offset begin [end]
```  
Specifies to return records in the file offset range specified with the begin and end values. When you specify begin and end , the tool returns all records between and including these points. If you do not specify end , then the utility returns the record at begin or immediately after begin only.  
```
-short [ num_points ]
```  
Specifies that the utility returns up to num\_points of each polygon, path, or random repetition point. If you do not specify num\_points , then the utility does not return any points. For num\_points , specify a non-negative integer.  
<!-- image -->

## Description  
Runs the OASIS compliance checking tool on your OASIS file in order to help diagnose any problems in your files.

## Examples  
```
#To get a record at specified offset 28: oasis_info doc/fw/tut3/NAND.oasis -offset 28 ... 28     PROPERTY:28   ref 0  'OASIS_LIB_REVISION' cnt 1 pr:str(tp:14 ref:0) 'Synopsys OASIS Library R-2020.09-SP1.807894' ... #To get records in a range 13-40: oasis_info doc/fw/tut3/NAND.oasis -offset 13 40 ... 13    START       unit=1000.000000 table_offset at <END> record 28     PROPERTY:28   ref 0  'OASIS_LIB_REVISION' cnt 1 pr:str(tp:14 ref:0) 'Synopsys OASIS Library R-2020.09-SP1.807894' 33     PROPERTY:28   ref 1  'SYNOPSYS_SEG_FW' cnt 6 pr:str(tp:15 ref:1) 'version' pr:str(tp:14 ref:2) 'R-2020.09-SP1 (841427)' pr:str(tp:15 ref:3) 'layout_server_version' pr:str(tp:13 ref:2) 'R-2020.09-SP1 (841427)' pr:str(tp:15 ref:4) 'compression'  pr:uint 6 ... #To get all records in a CBLOCK at specified offset 50: oasis_info doc/fw/tut3/NAND.oasis -cblock 50 ... 50    CBLOCK:34      CBLOCK     comp-bytes 92 uncomp-bytes 118 rate=77.97% C:0    XYRELATIVE:16 C:1    PLACEMENT:17  x 480 y 1170 flp 0 mag 1.0 ang 0 ref 1  'ACONT' rep:3 y-dm:1 y-sp:120 C:11   PLACEMENT:17  x 240 y 1170 flp 0 mag 1.0 ang 0 ref 1  'ACONT' rep:3 y-dm:1 y-sp:120 C:16   PLACEMENT:17  x 720 y 1170 flp 0 mag 1.0 ang 0 ref 1  'ACONT' rep:3 y-dm:1 y-sp:120 ... #To get a record from a CBLOCK (offset 50) at specified offset 11: oasis_info doc/fw/tut3/NAND.oasis -cblock 50 -offset 11 ... 50    CBLOCK:34      CBLOCK     comp-bytes 92 uncomp-bytes 118 rate=77.97% C:11   PLACEMENT:17  x 240 y 1170 flp 0 mag 1.0 ang 0 ref 1  'ACONT' rep:3 y-dm:1 y-sp:120 ...
```

metadata.Header 2: Creating Standalone Cache Files with genCache

content:
## Creating Standalone Cache Files with genCache  
This appendix describes the application used to generate standalone cache files for GDSII, GDSII gzip files, OASIS, and OASIS gzip files.  
These topics are available:  
- runProg genCache
- Using the genCache DP Option

## runProg genCache  
The genCache tool is available in the /ICVWB\_INSTALL\_DIR/bin directory. You can generate a cache file without starting a session using the runProg genCache ca he fil g n r t tool from the terminal window.
## Syntax

## For Linux:  
```
runP og e Cach runProg genCache inputFileName directoryOfOutputCacheFile [-64][-f][-cores number ] [-dp host_file [-dp_workers workers_number ]] [-layout_oasis_strict on|off] [-reference_propertieson|off] [-mode hicap|locap] [-max_warnings number |all][-progress] [-path_close_smooth on|off]
```

## For Windows:  
```
genCach . x genCache.exe inputFileName directoryOfOutputCacheFile [-64] [-f][-cores number ] [-dp host_file [-dp_workers workers_number ]] [-layout_oasis_strict on|off] [-reference_propertieson|off] [-mode hicap|locap] [-max_warnings number |all][-progress] [-path_close_smooth on|off]
```

## Arguments  
inputFileName  
Specifies the layout (OASIS or GDSII) file for which you want cache file information generated.  
directoryOfOutputCacheFile  
Specifies the directory where you want the output cache file located.  
-64  
Specifies to use the 64-bit server when parsing a 64-bit OASIS file. If you do not specify this argument, the tool uses the 32-bit server instead. Note that specifying this argument might cause the tool to use more memory at runtime.  
-f Force to regenerate a new cache file. Overwrite a cache file if it exists.  
```
-cores number
```  
An integer between 1 and 32 specifying the number of cores to be used. If this optional parameter is not specified, the number of available cores are used (up to 32).  
```
-dp host_file
```  
Specifies using d genCach distr bu p o istributed processing with the servers listed in host\_file .  
```
-dp_workers workers_number
```  
Specifies the number of workers used during distributed processing. The number of workers should be less than or equal to the total number of slots provided by host\_file . The default is 4 .  
```
-layout_oasis_strict on|off
```  
Allow to generate cache for illegal strict OASIS file that is actually not-strict. If set as on , genCache prints a warning and continues generating cache. If set as off , the application errors-out according to the OASIS specification requirements. Default is on .  
```
-reference_properties on|off
```  
Specifies whether to read instance properties before loading the layout. A Boolean. The default is on .  
```
-mode hicap|locap
```  
Allowed values are locap and hicap . hicap configures command for high speed, but increases the load time and uses more memory. The default is hicap .  
<!-- image -->  
when creating a cache file. The default is on .  
<!-- image -->  
```
-max_warnings number |all Specifies the maximum allowed warnings. The default is 5. -progress Display the percentage of completion of the cache file generation at the terminal. -path_close_smooth on|off Creates a smooth connection between the start and end of a closed path outline
```

## Description  
Cache files store information about the layout files, allowing the application to load them more quickly. This feature is especially useful when you previously opened a large layout file (that has not changed since the last run). Cache files can also be generated using distributed processing.

## Note:  
No new cache file is generated if the up-to-date cache file exists in the output directory. You can override this by specifying the -f flag.

## Examples  
Example 1 The following generates a cache file in your current working directory for the layout test.gds  
runProg genCache test.gds

## Example 2 Using layout strict mode:  
```
genCache inputFileName arg1 directoryOfOutputCacheFile arg2 -layout_oasis_strict on Same as: genCache inputFileName arg1 directoryOfOutputCacheFile arg2
```

## Using the genCache DP Option  
You can set up a distributed job for OASIS files by using the genCach DP opti s u d r b j genCache Distributed Processing (DP) option. DP cache generation enables you to generate cache files more quickly in cases where the file is located on a network server and many host machines are available.  
A distributed run requires interfacing to multiple hosts/nodes to launch Workers from a single Master application. The host machines for the Worker and Master should be dedicated and all hosts should have access to the layout file located on the network server.  
<!-- image -->

## The Host File  
A host file is used to provide host information to genCache. The following example demonstrates the formatting for a distr bu e p oc ngh f l xam host file in RSH mode:  
```
# HOSTS INFORMATION FILE (RSH) # Each valid host definition occupies an entire line. # Line with '#' as the first character is a comment line. # Format of each line: # # enabled| hostname| #slots| tmpDir| mode| command 1| teralab-x | 1 | /tmp| RSH | rsh 1| teralab-y | 1 | /tmp| RSH | rsh
```  
Table47 contains detailed information about the host file.  
Table 47 genCache Host File Information  
| Hosts Information File Details Field   | Value                                  | Purpose                                                                                                                                                         |
|----------------------------------------|----------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 1                                      | An integer - can be 0 or 1             | A 0 signifies that the host cannot be used. a 1 denotes a usable Worker machine.                                                                                |
| teralab-x                              | A string - a valid hostname            | This is the hostname of a valid Worker machine. For SGE, LSF this field is empty.                                                                               |
| 1                                      | An integer - any valid integer         | This number is used to denote the number of worker slots on this host (rsh and ssh) or farm (lsf and sge). -1 indicates unlimited. For genCache it should be 1. |
| /tmp                                   | A string - a valid, writable directory | This directory is used for local data storage for an application. GenCache is not using this.                                                                   |
| RSH                                    | A string - command mode                | The string signifies the command mode used to connect to the Worker machine. Valid entries are RSH, SSH, LSF, and SGE.                                          |
| rsh                                    | A string - the connection command      | The given string denotes the remote command used to connect to the Worker machine.                                                                              |

## The Log File  
genCache generates several log files in DP mode. These logs are informative and useful for understanding the interaction between the genCache master and workers.  
<!-- image -->  
The following log files are created for the genCache application run in DP mode:  
- master.<hostname>.<pid>.log
- worker.<hostname>.<pid>.log  
The number of Worker log files is equal to the number of Workers that ran during the DP loading. Use the -dp\_no\_worker\_logging command line option to disable Log files for Workers.  
The location of log files is affected by setting the CDPL\_LOGDIR environment variable. If this variable is not defined, the current working directory is used.  
The Number of Workers  
You should specify the number of workers to be used during DP genCache. The number of workers should be less than or equal to the total number of slots provided by the host information file. genCache uses 4 workers by default. You can specify the number of workers by using the -dp\_workers option.

## Examples  
```
genCache inputFileName directoryOfOutputCacheFile [-64] [-cores number] [-dp host_file [-dp_cmd worker_cmd] [-dp_workers workers_number] [-dp_no_worker_logging]]
```  
To set up a distributed job:

## 1. Create the host file.  
The host file should be formatted as shown in the following example:  
```
# host file sample containing 2 worker machines \ (my_server_1 and my_server_2) # and specifying rsh as connection mode 1 | my_server_1 | 1 | /tmp | RSH | rsh 1 | my_server_2 | 1 | /tmp | RSH | rsh
```

## 2. Define the log directory.  
This step is optional.

## Note:  
The log directory should be visible from all workers, that is, it should be network-visible. If you don't specify the log directory, then the current directory is used as the log directory. In this case, the current directory also should be network-visible.

## 3. Run the genCache command:  
```
runProg genCache test_layout.oasis cache_directory \ -dp host_file -dp_workers 2
```  
<!-- image -->

## Layout Format Conversion  
These topics are available:  
- Converting GDS and OASIS to Optimized OASIS
- Converting GDS and OASIS to Optimized OASIS in DP mode
- Converting OASIS to GDS

metadata.Header 2: Converting GDS and OASIS to Optimized OASIS

content:
## Converting GDS and OASIS to Optimized OASIS  
gds2oa i  ut l y The gds2oasis converter is a command-line utility that generates Optimized OASIS. Optimized OASIS is a legal OASIS-spec compliant OASIS file that any OASIS-compliant reader can read. Synopsys tools can load the Optimized OASIS instantly even when opening the layout for the first time (as if it had a cache file). Also, Optimized OASIS has better performance because of optimizations while converting the input layout. The gds2oasis utility is available in the /ICVWB\_INSTALL\_DIR/bin directory and needs to be run from the terminal window.
## Syntax

## For Linux  
gds2oa i ut l y gds2oasis parameters\_value input\_filename output\_filename

## For Windows  
gds2oasis.exe parameters\_value input\_filename output\_filename

## Returns  
1 on syntax/input error and 0 otherwise.

## Arguments  
parameters\_value  
Specifies a list of paired parameters and values, for example, {parameter1 value1 parameter2 value2 …}.  
<!-- image -->  
```
-dp host_file
```  
Specifies using distributed processing with the servers listed in host\_file .  
```
-dp_workers workers_number
```  
Specifies the number of workers used during distributed processing. The number of workers should be less than or equal to the total number of slots provided by host\_file . The default is 4.  
```
-dp_no_worker_logging
```  
Log file Workers can be disabled by using the -dp\_no\_worker\_logging command. For more information about using the Optimized OASIS DP options please see #unique\_364.

## Note:  
The Windows platform does not support DP options.  
```
-cores number
```  
Specifies the number of cores to be used during sorting and compaction. This argument accepts positive integers. If it is not specified, the number of cores is determined automatically.  
```
-cacheDir dir_name
```  
Specifies cache file directory for the layout servers used to open the input file. If this argument is not specified, the cache is switched off.  
```
-compress level
```  
Indicates the OASIS compression level. It accepts numbers from 0 to 9. 0 means no compression and no CBLOCKs are generated in this case. The default is 6.  
```
-omit_fig_properties
```  
If this argument is provided, properties of shapes and instances are not converted into the output OASIS OPT file. Otherwise, all shapes and instances properties are converted into the output file.  
```
-remove_duplicate_refs boolean
```  
When set to 1 , duplicate references are removed during the conversion of GDS and OASIS layouts to Optimized OASIS.  
```
-round_end_seg_count number
```  
Provides the number of vertices that should be used while converting round ends of paths to polygons. The default is 8. This argument accepts integers greater than or equal to 8.  
<!-- image -->  
```
-load_gdsii_boxes
```  
When the value is true, GDSII boxes are loaded as polygons and converted to a Optimized OASIS file. The default is false.  
```
-round_path
```  
Controls the rounding of corners for circular paths. When the value is true, the path corners are rounded along with the path ends. The default is false.  
```
-wind_path
```  
Specifies path winding. For a more detailed description, see the default windpath command in the IC Validator WorkBench Command Manual . The default is false.  
```
-path_close_smooth on|off
```  
Creates a smooth connection between the start and end of a closed path outline when converting GDS files to Optimized OASIS files.  
```
-progress
```  
Display at the terminal the completion percentage of the optimized layout file generation.  
```
input_filename
```  
Indicates the input layout file. It accepts all layout types supported by the applications.  
```
output_filename
```  
Indicates the output layout file, which is a spatially sorted valid OASIS file. No autocomplete for the file extension is applied.  
```
-nooptimize
```  
When the -nooptimize mode is used, a regular OASIS file is generated. In this mode, distributed processing is not available.

## Description  
Takes the input file and converts it to an optimized and spatially organized OASIS OPT file, which is a valid OASIS file with increased search performance.

metadata.Header 2: Converting GDS and OASIS to Optimized OASIS in DP mode

content:
## Converting GDS and OASIS to Optimized OASIS in DP mode  
The gds2oasis converter includes a DP option for GDSII files. This enables you to speed up Optimized OASIS conversion in cases where the file is located on a network server and many host machines are available.  
<!-- image -->  
The Host File  
Host machines for the Master and Workers should be dedicated. All hosts should have access to the layout file located on the network server. Then the host information file should be created.  
The Log File  
Optimized OASIS generates several log files in DP mode; this is similar to the Log File that generates the genCache in DP mode. For additional information, see Using the genCache DP Option.  
The Number of Workers  
You should specify the number of Workers to be used during DP Optimized OASIS conversion. The number of Workers should be less than or equal to the total number of slots provided by the host information file. Optimized OASIS uses four workers by default. You can specify the number of workers by using Optimized OASIS's -dp\_workers command line option.  
Additionally, you can pass regular gds2oasis options such as -compress or other private options.

## Converting OASIS to GDS  
The oasis2gds is a command-line script that is available in the /ICVWB\_INSTALL\_DIR/bin directory and performs OASIS to GDS conversions up to 40% faster when compared to opening and then saving the layout, and consumes up to 5% lesser memory. The syntax for the script is as follows:  
oasis2gds <input\_filename> <output\_filename>  
To use the oasis2gds script:  
1. Go to the ICVWB\_INSTALL\_DIR/bin directory.
2. Run the oasis2gds script from the Windows or Linux command-line. For example:  
```
ICVWB_INSTALL_DIR is the installation directory.
```  
```
◦ Windows: oasis2gds.bat layout1.oas layout2.gds ◦ Linux: oasis2gds layout1.oas layout2.gds
```  
<!-- image -->

## Using Python With the Application  
This appendix describes the using Python to script the application and using the iLayout Python module for working with layouts.  
These topics are available:  
- Python Scripting
- iLayout Python Module
- Boolean Operations on snps.ilayout Objects
- Creating Python GUI Widgets

## Python Scripting  
To start scripting ICVWB in Python, you need to first import snps.wb . All commands described in the ICVWB Command Manual-with the exception of those that explicitly require Tcl callbacks or objects, such as cell data , find init -data , bop commandsare available as functions.  
The function names follow a simple rule: spaces in the command name are replaced with underscores. For example, layout root cells -> layout\_root\_cells() .  
Here are some examples of working with the ICVWB application using Python:  
```
import snps.wb as wb wb.layout_new("a") wb.cell_object_add({'type':'rectangle','coords':[0,0,200,50]}) wb.layout_open("layouts/4bit.oas") [cell for cell in wb.layout_cells()] #-> ['1bit', '4bit'] bboxes=[wb.cell_bbox(cell=cell) for cell in wb.layout_cells()] bboxes[0] #-> [-15000000.0, -59000000.0, 83000000.0, 20000000.0]
```  
You can access Python script custom arguments (excluding the application-specific predefined arguments) using sys.argv , or access the full list of all arguments using snps.wb.argv .  
<!-- image -->

## Note:  
```
It is recommended to avoid known ICVWB parameters like -nodisplay , -cores , -help , and so on for your_script_args . These parameters are processed by ICVWB itself and might not be passed to your Python script in sys.argv .
```  
You can also use the Python Pane to access snps.ilayout : the iLayout Python module. The iLayout module is a simple yet powerful API for reading or writing layout files. See iLayout Python Module for more information.

## iLayout Python Module  
The snps.ilayout Python module provides a simple API for reading and writing layout data. The module currently supports GDSII, GDSII.gz, OASIS, and OASIS\_OPT formats. The implementation scales to very large layouts: it can read and write full-chip designs. There is no Python package for snps.ilayout . The module is included with IC Validator WorkBench and can be used from its Python Pane.

metadata.Header 2: Print basic information about an OASIS layout

content:
## Print basic information about an OASIS layout  
```
import snps.ilayout as il lout = il.open('/path/to/layout.oas') print(lout.dbu) print(lout.properties) print([cell.name for cell in lout])
```

## API Overview  
The module exports two main functions: open() and save() .  
snps.ilayout.open() loads a layout and returns a snps.ilayout.Layout object. The latter provides a cell iterator and each cell provides an iterator of elements.  
snps.ilayout.save() saves any object with expected attributes; sub-classing snps.ilayout.Layout is not needed (and not supported).

metadata.Header 2: Cell elements are of either of the following types:

content:
## Cell elements are of either of the following types:  
- snps.ilayout.Poly
- snps.ilayout.Path
- snps.ilayout.Ref
- snps.ilayout.Text  
<!-- image -->  
<!-- image -->  
All snps.ilayout objects (including Layout and Cell) are immutable. Modification is only done by creating a new object. The following example illustrates this. The example normalizes text elements by setting the magnification to 1.

## Normalize text element magnification  
```
import snps.ilayout as il def elem_normalized(elem): """ Normalizing the scales of il.Text objects by dropping the scale, i.e., default 1 is applied""" if type (elem) == il.Text: return il.Text(string=elem.string, location=elem.location, layer=elem.layer, dt=elem.dt, properties=elem.properties) return elem class cell_normalized: """ Cell with a given cell. """ def __init__(self, cell): self.cell = cell self.name = cell.name self.properties = cell.properties def __iter__(self): return (elem_normalized(elem) for elem in self.cell) class lout_normalized: """ Layout with a given layout. """ def __init__(self, layout): """ Builds a layout with the given layout. """ self.layout = layout self.properties = layout.properties self.dbu = layout.dbu def __iter__(self): """ Cell iterator """ return (cell_normalized(cell) for cell in self.layout) lout = il. open ('/path/to/layout.gds') il.save(lout_normalized(lout), 'normalize_text_mag.gds', format ='gds', dbu=lout.dbu)
```  
snps.ilayout.children() returns cell children as iterable objects of strings. snps.ilayout.bbox() returns a tuple of minimum and maximum points of given object. snps.ilayout.filter() returns cell objects as iterable objects.

content:
## Print the cell's children, bbox, and filtered layers  
```
import os import sys import snps.ilayout as il def parent_child(lout): """Generates (parent, child) pairs of cell names for the layout passed as argument.""" for cell in lout: for child in il.children(cell): yield (cell.name, child) def cells_bbox(lout): """Generates (cell_name, bbox) pairs of cell names for the layout passed as argument.""" for cell in lout: yield(cell.name, il.bbox(cell, lout)); def filter_layers(lout): """Generate layer iterator of given cell""" mylist = ((10,0),(11,0),(12,0),(13,0),(14,0)) yield(il.filter(il.filter.layer_dt(mylist), cell)) print("# Print every cell hierarchy for a1248.gds") file = f'/path/to/a1248.gds' layout = il.open(file) all_hier = parent_child(layout) for hier in all_hier: print(hier) all_bbox = cells_bbox(layout) for bbox in all_bbox: print(bbox) cell = next(iter(layout)) layers = filter_layers(cell) for layer in layers: print(layer) sys.exit()
```

## snps.ilayout.open (arg0: str, **kwargs) -> snps.ilayout.Layout  
Loads a layout (in GDSII, OASIS, OASIS\_OPT and GDSII.GZ formats) from the given file\_path and returns a Python object of type snps.ilayout.Layout . The first argument is the file\_path of the loaded layout; it is a string. The **kwargs are optional keyword arguments.  
The optional keyword arguments are:  
- cache\_dir: str  
Specifies the path of the directory for saving/reading the layout cache file. This argument accepts a ':' separated list of paths. When setting the cache directories with default layout\_cache\_dir or from Options > Layout > Cache in the graphic user interface, the application checks that there is a writable directory available in the cache paths, otherwise issues an error message. The first writable cache-directory is used for writing the cache-files. For more details, see the default layout\_cache\_dir command in the IC Validator WorkBench Command Manual .  
If you do not specify an argument, no cache file is created.  
- cores: int  
Specifies the maximal allowed layout load concurrency. You can specify an integer from one through the maximum of 256. If you specify more cores than the machine has, then the machine's core count is used instead. If you do not specify an argument the number of available cores is used. For more details, see the default layout\_oasis\_cores command in the IC Validator WorkBench Command Manual .

## Example:  
```
lout = il.open('/path/to/layout.gds', cache_dir= '/tmp/', cores=8)
```

following types: snps.ilayout.Poly , snps.ilayout.Path , snps.ilayout.Ref and snps.ilayout.Text .

## Layout Creation Example  
The following example shows a simple case of creating and saving a new layout.

## Simple layout creation  
```
import snps.ilayout as il class layout: """ Layout with a given list of cells. """ def __init__(self, cells): """ Builds a layout with the given cell list. """ self.dbu = 1e-9 self.properties = [] self.cells = cells def __iter__(self): """ Cell iterator """ return iter(self.cells) class cell: """ Cell with a given list of elements. """ def __init__(self, name, elems): """ Builds a cell with a given element list. """ self.elems = elems self.name = name def __iter__(self): """ Cell contents iterator""" return iter (self.elems) # Create a list of elements. elements = [il.Poly(boundary=[(0,0), (0,100), (100,100), (100,0)]), il.Poly(boundary=[(200,200), (200,300), (300, 300), (300,200)])] elements.append(il.Text(string='text', location=(250, 100), layer=5, dt=0)) # Create a cell with the above list of elements. new_cell = cell('a', elements) # Create a layout with new_cell. new_layout = layout([new_cell]) # Save new_layout in gds format. il.save(new_layout, 'new_created_layout.gds', dbu=new_layout.dbu, format='gds')
```

## Boolean Operations on snps.ilayout Objects  
The snps.pytbool module can be used to perform Boolean operations on snps.ilayout objects. The iLayout Python module is implemented with efficient layer/datatype filtering and cell flattening methods to support Boolean operations.  
- Functional Description
- Layer/datatype Filtering
- Flattening Cells  
<!-- image -->

## Functional Description  
Boolean operations take one or more iterables, which yield il.Poly objects, and the result is a similar iterable object. For example, snps.ilayout.Cell objects can be directly passed to pytBool operators.

## Note:  
When passing snps.ilayout.Cell objects to a pytbool operation, polygons from subcells are not part of the Boolean operation . If you want to perform the operation on the cell including polygons from placements, the cell should be flattened first, using, for example, snps.wb.layout\_extrac('-flat', ...) .

metadata.Header 2: The following Boolean operations are available:

content:
## The following Boolean operations are available:  
```
· snps.pytbool.and_(iterable1, iterable2) · snps.pytbool.or_(iterable1, iterable2) · snps.pytbool.xor_(iterable1, iterable2) · snps.pytbool.not_(iterable1, iterable2)
```

## Layer/datatype Filtering  
To restrict the Boolean operation to certain layers/datatypes, the following approach is recommended:  
```
iterable = il.filter(il.filter.layer_dt((10, 10)), cell)
```  
The following functions are implemented in the snps.ilayout module:

## Syntax  
```
snps.ilayout.filter.layer_dt()
```

## This takes either:  
- a Tuple[int, int]- a (layer, datatype) pair, or
- a List[Tuple[int, int]]- a list of layer/datatypes  
And produces a predicate object.

## Syntax  
```
snps.ilayout.filter()
```  
This takes a predicate object returned by snps.ilayout.filter.layer\_dt() and a Cell object. And returns a Cell object, which only iterates elements on the specified layers.  
<!-- image -->

## Example  
```
from snps import ilayout as il, pytbool as pb # Open a flat layout, get the (single) cell. lout = il.open('flat_lout.oas') cell = next(iter(lout)) # Filter layer/dt 1:0 and 2:0. lyr1 = il.filter(il.filter.layer_dt((1, 0)),  cell) lyr2 = il.filter(il.filter.layer_dt((2, 0)),  cell) # XOR lyr1 and lyr2. diff = pb.xor_(lyr1, lyr2) # Name the diff and save it. named_diff = name_cell(diff, 'XOR') il.save([named_diff], 'xor.oas', dbu=lout.dbu, format='oasis') class name_cell: """ Renames the orig cell with new name """ def __init__(self, orig, name): self.name = name self.orig = orig def __iter__(self): """ Cell contents iterator""" return iter(self.orig)
```

## Flattening Cells  
You can flatten cells using the iLayout Python feature. The snps.ilayout.flatten() method takes as arguments a cell-like object and a layout-like object and returns a flattened cell object.

## Syntax  
```
snps.ilayout.flatten(cell, layout) Arguments cell A cell-like object. layout A layout-like object. Example """ Function to drop all references to the cells """ def drop_refs (elem):
```  
<!-- image -->  
```
if type(elem) != il.Ref: return elem class layout: def __init__(self, cells): self.dbu = 1e-9 self.properties = [] self.cells = cells def __iter__(self): return iter(self.cells) class cell: def __init__(self, name, elems): self.elems = elems self.name = name def __iter__(self): return (drop_refs(elem) for elem in self.elems) import snps.ilayout as il import snps.pytbool as pb lout = il.open('/path/to/layout.oasis') my_cell=[c for c in lout if c.name == 'my_cell_name'][0] flat_cell = il.flatten(my_cell, layout=lout) newLayout = layout([cell("my_cell_name_flat", flat_cell)]) il.save(newLayout, 'flat.oas', dbu=1e-9, format='oasis')
```

## About This User Guide  
The Synopsys PrimeTime ® Suite provides comprehensive full-chip analysis of static timing, signal integrity, and full-chip power in a single integrated environment.  
This guide is for engineers who use the PrimeTime tool for static timing and signal integrity analysis. Readers should have some familiarity with static timing analysis principles.  
The PrimeTime Suite documentation consists of the following documents:  
- PrimeTime User Guide (this user guide) - Timing analysis using the PrimeTime, PrimeTime SI, PrimeTime ADV, and PrimeTime ADVP tools.
- PrimeClosure User Guide - High-capacity, AI-driven, RTL-to-GDSII ECO fixing with signoff-quality timing.
- PrimePower User Guide - Static and dynamic full-chip power analysis.
- PrimeShield User Guide - Parametric timing robustness analysis, cell robustness analysis, and critical path fast Monte Carlo HSPICE simulation.
- PrimeECO User Guide - ECO timing, power, and DRC fixing with signoff-quality timing.  
This preface includes the following sections:  
- New in This Release
- Related Products, Publications, and Trademarks
- Conventions
- Customer Support

## Introduction to PrimeTime  
The PrimeTime Suite performs full-chip, gate-level static timing analysis, an essential part of the design and analysis flow for chip designs. The tool exhaustively validates the timing performance of a design by checking all paths for timing violations, without using logic simulation or test vectors. To learn more about the basics of the PrimeTime tool, see  
- PrimeTime Capabilities
- PrimeTime Product Tiers and Licenses
- PrimeTime Add-On Tools
- Using PrimeTime in the Implementation Flow
- Compatibility With Synopsys Implementation Tools
- Overview of Static Timing Analysis

## PrimeTime Capabilities  
In PrimeTime, you can perform many types of design checks and analysis:

## · Design Checks  
- Setup, hold, recovery, and removal constraints
- User-specified data-to-data timing constraints
- Clock-gating setup and hold constraints
- Minimum period and minimum pulse width for clocks
- Design rules (minimum and maximum transition time, capacitance, and fanout)
- Analysis Features
- Multiple clocks and clock frequencies
- False path and multicycle path timing exceptions
- Transparent latch analysis and time borrowing
- Simultaneous minimum and maximum delay analysis for setup and hold constraints  
<!-- image -->  
<!-- image -->  
- Analysis with on-chip variation (OCV) of process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) conditions
- Case analysis of constants or specific transitions applied to specified inputs
- Mode analysis with module-specific operating modes, such as read mode or write mode for a RAM module
- Bottleneck analysis to report cells that cause the most timing violations
- Crosstalk analysis between physically adjacent nets
- Efficient hierarchical analysis using HyperScale technology
- Comprehensive constraint consistency checking
- Engineering change order (ECO) analysis that corrects violations and optimizes power by inserting buffers, resizing cells, and swapping cells

## PrimeTime Add-On Tools  
The PrimeTime Suite supports the following add-on features.  
- PrimeClosure - Provides a complete engineering change order (ECO) solution:
- Synopsys PrimeClosure is the next-generation signoff ECO solution, integrated with PrimeTime static timing analysis and Fusion Compiler RTL-to-GDSII implementation. It accelerates power-performance-area closure and features a unique architecture that handles demanding design capacity and advanced node process complexity issues on a single box.  
For more information, see the PrimeClosure User Guide .  
- PrimePower - Supports advanced power analysis:
- The PrimePower add-on tool analyzes full-chip power dissipation of cell-based designs. It supports both vector-free and vector-based peak power and average power analysis.  
For more information, see the PrimePower User Guide .  
<!-- image -->  
- PrimeShield - Supports parametric robustness analysis:
- PrimeShield provides design robustness analysis and fixing in the presence of increased process and voltage variability at advanced nodes, and enables designers to minimize pessimism, over-margining, and over-design to effectively reduce power and boost maximum operating frequency.  
For more information, see the PrimeShield User Guide .  
- PrimeECO - Supports engineering change order (ECO) implementation and analysis:
- The PrimeECO add-on tool has been replaced by the PrimeClosure tool.

metadata.Header 2: Using PrimeTime in the Implementation Flow

content:
## Using PrimeTime in the Implementation Flow  
The PrimeTime tool works well with other Synopsys tools such as Design Compiler, ICCompilerII, Fusion Compiler, and StarRC. These tools share many of the same libraries, databases, and commands, as shown in the following figure.  
<!-- image -->  
Figure 1 Implementation Flow With PrimeTime Analysis  
<!-- image -->  
Starting from an RTL design, the Design Compiler tool generates a gate-level design. From the gate-level netlist and physical library information, the physical implementation tool (ICCompilerII) performs placement and routing. The StarRC parasitic extraction tool extracts the parasitic RC data from the chip layout database.  
<!-- image -->  
<!-- image -->  
The PrimeTime tool reads the gate-level netlist and parasitic data, and verifies the design timing using information provided in the logic (.db) library. If the tool finds any violations, it can generate engineering change orders (ECOs) that guide the physical implementation tool to fix the violations and optimize power.  
PrimeTime can also operate as a standalone static timing analyzer in other design flows.

## Compatibility With Synopsys Implementation Tools  
The PrimeTime static timing analysis tool is designed to work well with the Design Compiler synthesis tool and the ICCompilerII place-and-route tool. These tools are compatible in the following ways:  
- They use the same logic libraries and read the same design data files.
- They support the Synopsys Design Constraints (SDC) format for specifying design constraints, including the timing and area constraints.
- They share many commands (such as create\_clock , set\_input\_delay , and report\_timing ) that are identical or similar in operation.
- They share the same delay calculation algorithms and produce similar delay results.
- They generate similar timing reports.
- PrimeTime can provide engineering change order (ECO) guidance to ICCompilerII by generating change lists that fix timing violations and optimize power.  
Although the Design Compiler and ICCompilerII tools have their own built-in static timing analysis capabilities, the PrimeTime tool has better speed, accuracy, capacity, and flexibility for static timing analysis. The PrimeTime tool also provides many features not supported by the other tools.

## See Also  
- Using PrimeTime With Design Compiler

## Overview of Static Timing Analysis  
Static timing analysis is a method of validating the timing performance of a design by checking all possible paths for timing violations. PrimeTime breaks a design down into timing paths, calculates the signal propagation delay along each path, and checks for violations of timing constraints inside the design and at the input/output interface.  
Another way to perform timing analysis is to use dynamic simulation, which determines the full behavior of the circuit for a given set of input stimulus vectors. Compared to dynamic simulation, static timing analysis is much faster because it is not necessary to simulate the logical operation of the circuit. Static timing analysis is also more thorough because it checks all timing paths, not just the logical conditions that are sensitized by a particular set of test vectors. However, static timing analysis can only check the timing, not the functionality, of a circuit design.  
<!-- image -->

## Timing Paths  
When performing timing analysis, PrimeTime first breaks down the design into timing paths. Each timing path consists of the following elements:  
- Startpoint - The start of a timing path where data is launched by a clock edge or where the data must be available at a specific time. Every startpoint must be either an input port or a register clock pin.
- Combinational logic network - Elements that have no memory or internal state. Combinational logic can contain AND, OR, XOR, and inverter elements, but cannot contain flip-flops, latches, registers, or RAM.
- Endpoint - The end of a timing path where data is captured by a clock edge or where the data must be available at a specific time. Every endpoint must be either a register data input pin or an output port.  
The following figure shows the timing paths in a simple design example.  
Figure 2 Timing paths  
<!-- image -->  
In the example, each logic cloud represents a combinational logic network. Each path starts at a data launch point, passes through some combinational logic, and ends at a data capture point.  
<!-- image -->  
| Path   | Startpoint                        | Endpoint                           |
|--------|-----------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| Path 1 | Input port                        | Data input of sequential element   |
| Path 2 | Clock pin of a sequential element | Data input of a sequential element |
| Path 3 | Clock pin of a sequential element | Output port                        |
| Path 4 | Input port                        | Output port                        |  
A combinational logic cloud might contain multiple paths, as shown in the following figure. PrimeTime uses the longest path to calculate a maximum delay and the shortest path to calculate a minimum delay.  
Figure 3 Multiple paths through combinational logic  
<!-- image -->  
PrimeTime also considers the following types of paths for timing analysis:  
- Clock path - A path from a clock input port or cell pin, through one or more buffers or inverters, to the clock pin of a sequential element; for data setup and hold checks.
- Clock-gating path - A path from an input port to a clock-gating element; for clock-gating setup and hold checks.
- Asynchronous path - A path from an input port to an asynchronous set or clear pin of a sequential element; for recovery and removal checks.  
Figure 4 Types of paths considered for timing analysis  
<!-- image -->

## Delay Calculation  
After breaking down a design into a set of timing paths, the PrimeTime tool calculates the delay along each path. The total delay of a path is the sum of all cell and net delays in the path.

## Cell Delay  
Cell delay is the amount of delay from input to output of a logic gate in a path. In the absence of back-annotated delay information from an SDF file, the tool calculates the cell delay from delay tables provided in the logic library for the cell.  
Typically, a delay table lists the amount of delay as a function of one or more variables, such as input transition time and output load capacitance. From these table entries, the tool calculates each cell delay. When necessary, PrimeTime uses interpolation or extrapolation of table values to obtain a delay value for the current conditions specified for the design.

## Net Delay  
Net delay is the amount of delay from the output of a cell to the input of the next cell in a timing path. This delay is caused by the parasitic capacitance of the interconnection between the two cells, combined with net resistance and the limited drive strength of the cell driving the net.  
<!-- image -->  
The PrimeTime tool calculates net delays with the following methods:  
- Estimating delays from a wire load model; this method is used before layout, when the chip topography is unknown
- Using specific time values back-annotated from a Standard Delay Format (SDF) file
- Using detailed parasitic resistance and capacitance data back-annotated from a Galaxy Parasitic Database (GPD), Standard Parasitic Exchange Format (SPEF), Detailed Standard Parasitic Format (DSPF), Reduced Standard Parasitic Format (RSPF) file

## Constraint Checks  
After PrimeTime determines the timing paths and calculates the path delays, it checks for violations of timing constraints, such as setup and hold constraints:  
- A setup constraint specifies how much time is necessary for data to be available at the input of a sequential device before the clock edge that captures the data in the device. This constraint enforces a maximum delay on the data path relative to the clock edge.
- A hold constraint specifies how much time is necessary for data to be stable at the input of a sequential device after the clock edge that captures the data in the device. This constraint enforces a minimum delay on the data path relative to the clock edge.  
In addition to setup and hold constraints, PrimeTime can also check recovery and removal constraints, data-to-data constraints, clock-gating setup and hold constraints, and the minimum pulse width for clock signals.  
The amount of time by which a violation is avoided is called the slack . For example, for a setup constraint, if a signal must reach a cell input at no later than 8 ns and is determined to arrive at 5 ns, the slack is 3 ns. A slack of 0 means that the constraint is just barely satisfied. A negative slack indicates a timing violation.

metadata.Header 2: Example of Setup and Hold Checks for Flip-Flops

content:
## Example of Setup and Hold Checks for Flip-Flops  
The following example shows how PrimeTime checks setup and hold constraints for a flipflop.  
<!-- image -->  
Figure 5 Setup and hold checks  
<!-- image -->  
For this example, assume that the flip-flops are defined in the logic library to have a minimum setup time of 1.0 time units and a minimum hold time of 0.0 time units. The clock period is defined in the tool to be 10 time units. The time unit size, such as ns or ps, is specified in the logic library.  
By default, the tool assumes that signals are propagated through each data path in one clock cycle. Therefore, when the tool performs a setup check, it verifies that the data launched from FF1 reaches FF2 within one clock cycle, and arrives at least 1.0 time unit before the data gets captured by the next clock edge at FF2. If the data path delay is too long, it is reported as a timing violation. For this setup check, the tool considers the longest possible delay along the data path and the shortest possible delay along the clock path between FF1 and FF2.  
When the tool performs a hold check, it verifies that the data launched from FF1 reaches FF2 no sooner than the capture clock edge for the previous clock cycle. This check ensures that the data already existing at the input of FF2 remains stable long enough after the clock edge that captures data for the previous cycle. For this hold check, the tool considers the shortest possible delay along the data path and the longest possible delay along the clock path between FF1 and FF2. A hold violation can occur if the clock path has a long delay.  
<!-- image -->  
<!-- image -->

metadata.Header 2: Example of Setup and Hold Checks for Latches

content:
## Example of Setup and Hold Checks for Latches  
Latch-based designs typically use two-phase, nonoverlapping clocks to control successive registers in a data path. In these cases, PrimeTime can use time borrowing to reduce the constraints on successive paths.  
For example, consider the two-phase, latch-based path shown in the following figure. All three latches are level-sensitive, with the gate active when the G input is high. The L1 and L3 latches are controlled by PH1, and the L2 latch is controlled by PH2. A rising edge launches data from the latch output, and a falling edge captures data at the latch input. In this example, consider the latch setup and delay times to be zero.  
Figure 6 Latch-based paths  
<!-- image -->  
<!-- image -->  
For the path from L1 to L2, the rising edge of PH1 launches the data. The data must arrive at L2 before the falling edge of PH2 at time = 20. This timing requirement is labeled Setup 1. Depending on the amount of delay between L1 and L2, the data might arrive either before or after the rising edge of PH2 at time = 10, as indicated by the dashed-line arrows labeled 'Arrival a' and 'Arrival b' in the timing diagram. Arrival after time = 20 is a timing violation.  
If the data arrives at L2 before the rising edge of PH2 at time = 10 (Arrival a), the data for the next path from L2 to L3 gets launched by the rising edge of PH2 at time = 10, just as a synchronous flip-flop operates. In this case, no time is borrowed from the second path. This timing requirement for L2 to L3 is labeled Setup 2a.  
If the data arrives after the rising edge of PH2 (Arrival b), the first path (from L1 to L2) borrows time from the second path (from L2 to L3). In that case, the launch of data for the second path occurs not at the rising edge, but at the data arrival time at L2, at some time between the rising and falling edges of PH2. This timing requirement is labeled Setup 2b. When borrowing occurs, the path originates at the D pin rather than the G pin of L2.  
For the first path (from L1 to L2), PrimeTime reports the setup slack as zero if borrowing occurs. The slack is positive if the data arrives before the rising edge at time=10, or negative (a violation) if the data arrives after the falling edge at time=20.  
To perform hold checking, PrimeTime considers the launch and capture edges relative to the setup check, as shown in the following figure. It verifies that data launched at the startpoint does not reach the endpoint too quickly, thereby ensuring that data launched in the previous cycle is latched and not overwritten by the new data.  
Figure 7 Hold checks in latch-based paths  
<!-- image -->

## Timing Exceptions  
If certain paths are not intended to operate according to the default setup and hold behavior assumed by the PrimeTime tool, you need to specify those paths as timing exceptions. Otherwise, the tool might incorrectly report those paths as having timing violations.  
<!-- image -->  
The PrimeTime tool lets you specify the following types of exceptions:  
- False path - A path that is never sensitized due to the logic configuration, expected data sequence, or operating mode.
- Multicycle path - A path designed to take more than one clock cycle from launch to capture.
- Minimum or maximum delay path - A path that must meet a delay constraint that you explicitly specify as a time value.  
For more information, see Chapter8, Timing Paths and Exceptions.

metadata.Header 2: Installing the PrimeTime Software and Licenses

content:
## Installing the PrimeTime Software and Licenses  
Before you can use the PrimeTime tool, you must install the software and licenses for your site. For information, see the following guides:  
- Synopsys Installation Guide at http://www.synopsys.com/install
- Synopsys Licensing Quickstart Guide at http://www.synopsys.com/licensing  
<!-- image -->

## Configuring the PrimeTime Work Environment  
When you start a PrimeTime session, the tool executes the commands in the PrimeTime setup files. In these files, you can initialize parameters, set variables, specify the design environment, and configure your preferred working options.  
The setup files have the same name, .synopsys\_pt.setup, but reside in different directories. PrimeTime reads the files from three directories in the following order:  
1. The Synopsys root directory ($SYNOPSYS/admin/setup)  
This system-wide setup file contains  
- System variables defined by Synopsys
- General PrimeTime setup information for all users at your site  
Only the system administrator can modify this file.  
2. Your home directory  
In this user-defined setup file, you can specify your preferences for the PrimeTime working environment. The variable settings in this file override the corresponding variable settings in the system-wide setup file.  
3. The current working directory from which you start PrimeTime  
In this design-specific setup file, you can specify project or design environment. The variable settings in this file override the corresponding variable settings in the userdefined and system-wide setup files.  
To suppress the execution of all .synopsys\_pt.setup files, use the -no\_init option when you start the tool with the pt\_shell command.

## Starting a PrimeTime Session  
You can start a PrimeTime session in either the command-line interface or the graphical user interface:  
- For the command-line interface, enter the following command at the Linux shell prompt:  
```
% pt_shell
```  
```
PrimeTime (R) Version M-2018.06 for linux64 - May 16, 2018 Copyright (c) 1988 - 201 Synopsys, Inc. This software and the associated documentation are proprietary ...
```  
<!-- image -->  
```
pt_shell>
```  
- For the graphical user interface (GUI), enter this command:  
```
% pt_shell -gui
```  
Figure 8 PrimeTime GUI window  
<!-- image -->

## See Also  
- Graphical User Interface

## License Checkouts  
When you start a PrimeTime session, the tool automatically checks out a PrimeTime license.  
During analysis, the tool automatically checks out additional licenses as needed, depending on the tool features used. An information message indicates when this occurs:  
```
Information: Checked out license 'PrimeTime-SI' (PT-019)
```  
To view the number of licenses currently checked out, use the list\_licenses command:  
```
pt_shell> list_licenses Licenses in use:
```  
<!-- image -->  
```
PrimeTime   (1) PrimeTime-SI   (1) 1
```  
Many additional features are available to control how licenses are used. For details, see Controlling License Behaviors.

## Entering pt\_shell Commands  
You interact with the tool by using pt\_shell commands, which are based on the Tool Command Language (Tcl). The PrimeTime command language provides capabilities similar to Linux command shells, including variables, conditional execution of commands, and control flow commands. To run the PrimeTime tool, you can  
- Enter individual commands interactively at the pt\_shell prompt
- Enter individual commands interactively on the console command line in the GUI
- Run one or more Tcl command scripts, which are text files containing pt\_shell commands  
For general information about the Tcl command-line interface, see Using Tcl With Synopsys Tools , available on SolvNetPlus.

## Using Python in pt\_shell  
You can use Python in the pt\_shell for interacting with the tool. Applications that support Python include both a Tcl and a Python console. The console language is selected by setting the sh\_language application variable. When the console language is Python, this is indicated by -py at the end of the prompt string.  
For example:  
```
pt_shell> set_app_var sh_language python
```  
The prompt changes to pt\_shell-py> .  
Now, you can use Python syntax (statements and expressions) to control the tool.  
To change the language back to Tcl, use  
```
pt_shell> cmd.set_app_var('sh_language', 'tcl')
```  
The prompt changes back to pt\_shell>  
All application commands, Tcl built-in commands, and user Tcl procedures are accessed by calling methods on the snps.cmd object. The method name is the same as the name of the Tcl command or procedure. If you want to evaluate Tcl scripts or files, use the cmd.eval or cmd.source method.  
<!-- image -->  
<!-- image -->

metadata.Header 2: Getting Help on the Command Line

content:
## Getting Help on the Command Line  
To get help when running the PrimeTime tool, use the following resources:  
- Command help
- To list all PrimeTime commands, organized by command group, enter pt\_shell> help
- To show a brief description of a command, enter pt\_shell> help command\_name
- To show all options and arguments for a command, enter pt\_shell> help -verbose command\_name
- Man pages  
To display the man page of a command, variable, or message, enter  
```
pt_shell> man command_variable_or_message_name
```  
To open the man page in an HTML Web browser, use the -html option of the man command.

For scripts that you can use as a starting point to implement the PrimeTime static timing analysis flow, see the Synopsys Reference Methodology System at https:// solvnet.synopsys.com/rmgen.

## Using Tcl/Tk in PrimeTime  
The PrimeTime command interface is based on Tool Command Language (Tcl) and the Tk toolkit, which is used in many other Synopsys tools. For general information about Tcl and its usage in Synopsys command shells, see Using Tcl With Synopsys Tools , available on SolvNetPlus.  
To see the Tcl/Tk version used by your version of the PrimeTime tool, enter  
```
pt_shell> printvar tcl_version tcl_version   = "8.6"
```

## Tcl Packages and Autoload  
The PrimeTime tool supports the standard Tcl package and autoload facilities. However, the load command is not supported, so packages that require shared libraries cannot be used. The tool is shipped with the standard implementations of the packages that are part of the Tcl distribution. For reference, you can find these packages below the Synopsys installation root directory in the auxx/tcllib/lib/tcl8.6 directory.  
To add a new Tcl package to PrimeTime, do one of the following actions:  
- Install the package into the Synopsys tree.
- In the .synopsys\_pt.setup setup file, add a new directory to the auto\_path variable.  
PrimeTime provides these default locations for loading packages into the application:  
- For application-specific Tcl packages, auxx/tcllib/primetime
- For packages that work with all Tcl-based Synopsys tools, auxx/tcllib/snps\_tcl  
For example, if you have a Tcl package called mycompanyPT that contains PrimeTime reporting facilities used by mycompany, you create a directory called mycompanyPT under the auxx/tcllib/primetime directory and then put the pkgIndex.tcl file and Tcl source files for the package into that directory. You can use the package in your PrimeTime scripts by using the following command:  
<!-- image -->  
<!-- image -->  
package require ecompanyPT

The PrimeTime tool supports the incr Tcl (itcl) extension, which adds object-oriented programming constructs to Tcl.  
For information about incr Tcl, see the Tcl Developer Xchange website at http://tcl.tk

metadata.Header 2: Checking and Compiling Scripts With the TclPro Toolkit

content:
## Checking and Compiling Scripts With the TclPro Toolkit  
TclPro is an open-source toolkit for Tcl programming that supports the following:  
- Checking the Syntax in Scripts With the TclPro Checker
- Creating Bytecode-Compiled Scripts With the TclPro Compiler
- Debugging Scripts With the TclPro Debugger  
For more information about the TclPro tools, go to http://tcl.sourceforge.net.

## Installing TclPro Tools  
Before using the TclPro tools, you need to install TclPro on your system. After you do this, specify the path to the installed program by setting the SNPS\_TCLPRO\_HOME environment variable. For example, if you installed TclPro version 1.5 at /u/tclpro1.5, set the SNPS\_TCLPRO\_HOME environment variable to point to that directory. The PrimeTime tool uses this variable as a base for launching some of the TclPro tools. In addition, other Synopsys applications use this variable to link to the TclPro tools.

metadata.Header 2: Checking the Syntax in Scripts With the TclPro Checker

content:
## Checking the Syntax in Scripts With the TclPro Checker  
The Synopsys Syntax Checker, based on the TclPro Checker (procheck), helps you find syntax and semantic errors in your Tcl scripts. Everything that you need for syntax and semantic checking is shipped with PrimeTime; it is not necessary to download the TclPro tools to access syntax checking.  
The Synopsys Syntax Checker, snps\_checker, checks the following:  
- Unknown options
- Ambiguous option abbreviation  
- Use of exclusive options
- Missing required options
- Validation of literal option values for numerical range (range, <=, >=)
- Validation of one-of-string (keyword) options
- Recursion into constructs that have script arguments, such as the redirect and foreach\_in\_collection commands
- Warning of duplicate options overriding previous values

## Running the Synopsys Syntax Checker  
There are two ways to run snps\_checker in the Synopsys environment. You can launch snps\_checker from the PrimeTime tool or run it standalone.  
To run snps\_checker standalone, use the wrapper scripts provided with the PrimeTime installation; running snps\_checker directly does not work. For the linux64 platform, you can find the script in the PrimeTime installation directory as linux64/syn/bin/ptprocheck.  
To launch snps\_checker from PrimeTime, you need to load a package provided with the installation as follows:  
```
package require snpsTclPro
```  
This makes the check\_script command available. Pass the name of the script you want to check to the check\_script command.  
The following example is a script with errors that is tested in snps\_checker:  
```
create_clock [get_ports CLK] -period create_clock [get_ports CLK] -period -12.2 sort_collection set paths [get_timing_paths -nworst 10 -delay_type mx_fall -r] my_report -from [sort_collection \ [sort_collection $a b] {b c d} -x] foreach_in_collection x $objects { query_objects $x report_timing -through $x -through $y -from a -from b -to z > r.out } all_fanout -from X -clock_tree puts [pwd xyz]
```  
The script loads the extensions shipped with your release. The following output example shows the loaded Synopsys extensions. Each line in the output shows where a syntax or semantic error was detected. The report indicates invalid syntax with a caret (^) below the character that begins the invalid syntax.  
<!-- image -->

## Example 1 snps\_checker Output  
<!-- image -->  
```
% /synopsys/linux64/syn/bin/ptprocheck ex1.tcl Synopsys Tcl Syntax Checker - Version 1.0 Loading snps_tcl.pcx... Loading primetime.pcx... scanning: /disk/scripts/ex1.tcl checking: /disk/scripts/ex1.tcl /disk/scripts/ex1.tcl:1 (warnUndefProc) undefined procedure: get_ports get_ports CLK ^ /disk/scripts/ex1.tcl:1 (SnpsE-MisVal) Value not specified for 'create_clock -period' create_clock [get_ports CLK] -period ^ /disk/scripts/ex1.tcl:2 (SnpsE-BadRange) Value -12.2 for 'create_clock -period' must be >= 0.000000 create_clock [get_ports CLK] -period -12.2 ^ /disk/scripts/ex1.tcl:3 (SnpsE-MisReq) Missing required positional options for sort_collection: collection criteria sort_collection ^ /disk/scripts/ex1.tcl:4 (badKey) invalid keyword "mx_fall" must be: max min min_max max_rise max_fall min_rise min_fall get_timing_paths -nworst 10 -delay_type mx_fall -r ^ /disk/scripts/ex1.tcl:4 (SnpsE-AmbOpt) Ambiguous option 'get_timing_paths -r' get_timing_paths -nworst 10 -delay_type mx_fall -r ^ /disk/scripts/ex1.tcl:5 (warnUndefProc) undefined procedure: my_report my_report -from [sort_collection \ ^ /disk/scripts/ex1.tcl:5 (SnpsE-UnkOpt) Unknown option 'sort_collection -x' sort_collection \ [sort_collection $a b] {b c d} -x ^ /disk/scripts/ex1.tcl:9 (SnpsW-DupOver) Duplicate option 'report_timing -from' overrides previous value report_timing -through $x -through $y -from a -from b -to z > r.out ^
```

metadata.Header 2: Limitations of the Synopsys Syntax Checker

content:
## Limitations of the Synopsys Syntax Checker  
The Synopsys Syntax Checker has the following limitations:  
- Command abbreviation is not checked. Abbreviated commands show up as undefined procedures.
- Aliases created with the alias command are not expanded and show up as undefined procedures.
- A few checks done when the application is running might not be checked. For example, some cases where one option requires another option are not checked.
- It cannot check extremely large scripts.
- PrimeTime allows you to specify Verilog-style bus names on the command line without rigid quoting, for instance, A[0]. This format with indexes from 0 to 255 is checked. Wildcards * and % are also checked. Other forms, including ranges as A[15:0] show as undefined procedures, unless represented as {A[15:0]}.
- User-defined procedures enhanced with the define\_proc\_attributes command are not checked. Because such procedures are declared with the args argument, no semantic errors are reported.
